principle: A Terraform plan is a captured, time-bound authorization, not a preview
because: Applying a saved plan file happens without prompting because passing the file is itself the approval — this is what turns the four-step init/plan/review/apply pipeline into a real control rather than a formality, and why reviewers must see plan output itself rather than an HCL diff. Manual review is where destructive changes get a human gate; the saved artifact carrying that approval is itself sensitive; and a reviewed plan going stale, together with the GitLab incident where 617 resources were destroyed by applying a plan approved three weeks earlier, shows what happens when the authorization is exercised after the world it was captured against has already changed.

members.subject: Manual plan review is recommended whenever changes could be destructive
members.description: HashiCorp's own automation guidance states that manual review of a plan is always recommended when Terraform could make destructive changes to infrastructure, unless the team can tolerate downtime from an unintended change — auto-approval is not the default recommendation for anything where damage is possible.

members.subject: -lock=false silently removes the concurrency safety net
members.description: Most Terraform commands accept -lock=false to skip acquiring the state lock; it's offered as an escape hatch for a stuck pipeline, but HashiCorp's own documentation explicitly recommends against it because it reopens the exact concurrent-write risk locking exists to prevent. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment, for consistency: T3-006 (force-unlock on a held lock -> multiple writers) and this row (-lock=false -> the same multiple-writer hazard) cite the same doc page about the same hazard and had landed at different levels. -lock=false runs successfully; the concurrent-write damage surfaces later, which is judgment. T3-006 was the correctly-assigned one.]

members.subject: Applying a saved plan file is unprompted; passing the file is the approval
members.description: The pipeline shape in T3-020 (init, plan, human review, apply) is only sound if apply consumes the reviewed artifact rather than recomputing one. Terraform supports this by writing a plan to a file with plan -out=FILE and applying that file directly, and when a saved plan file is passed to terraform apply, Terraform performs the operations in that saved plan without prompting for confirmation -- the docs state that passing the plan file is itself interpreted as the approval. This is the operational rule that makes plan/apply review discipline mean anything, and it is also why a stale saved plan executes with no second gate in front of it (see T3-023 and the GitLab incident in T3-037): the approval was captured weeks earlier, at plan time.

members.subject: Scoping state/workspace boundaries to limit blast radius
members.description: Because any write operation against a state file can affect every resource tracked in it, HCP Terraform's own guidance is to keep each workspace's state small and scoped to logically related resources rather than grouping unrelated infrastructure (e.g. compute and database) into one state file - the state boundary is a risk-containment decision, not just an organizational convenience.

members.subject: Reviewing plan output, not just HCL diffs, before merge
members.description: For a team, the value of terraform plan is as a review artifact, not just a preview: pairing plan output with the pull request lets reviewers see exactly what will change, ask questions, and catch mistakes that reading the HCL diff alone would miss, since HCL changes and their real infrastructure effects aren't always obvious from the code.

members.subject: Purpose of Terraform state
members.description: Terraform state exists to bind objects that already exist in a remote system to the resource instances declared in configuration, so Terraform can determine what already exists without re-inspecting the real infrastructure on every run. This binding function is why state must be tracked accurately and shared across a team rather than reasoned about locally.

members.subject: S3 backend native state-lockfile locking is opt-in, not automatic
members.description: State locking on the S3 backend is opt-in, not automatic, and as of current docs is implemented via a lockfile mechanism configured with the use_lockfile argument, distinct from the older DynamoDB-table-based approach. A team that copies a bare S3 backend block without adding either gets zero protection against concurrent writers and won't discover it until two applies collide. [Stage 2 depth correction: reclassified from mechanism to operation after merging a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-038, which cited the identical quote at depth operation. See merge log.]

members.subject: State file contents are sensitive by default
members.description: Terraform's state file stores a JSON snapshot of every managed resource, including secrets, passwords, and other sensitive attribute values in plaintext, so it must be treated as sensitive data with restricted access and encrypted, versioned remote storage - not committed to source control or left world-readable in a bucket. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: identical reasoning to T3-022 and T3-003 -- three rows making one claim ('Terraform writes your secrets somewhere in cleartext, so control access to it') should not sit at two different depths. T3-003 was already moved to judgment by Stage 2 on this exact reasoning.]

members.subject: Static provider credentials are a risk even with rotation
members.description: HCP Terraform's own docs frame static credentials as a security risk in themselves, not just a risk when unrotated — the guidance explicitly states rotating static credentials regularly does not eliminate the risk, which is the stated motivation for using OIDC-based dynamic credentials instead. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-041 ("OIDC/dynamic credentials vs. static long-lived credentials"), which cited the identical quote. See merge log.]

principle: Stripe's dated versions, Google's stability channels, and Buf's strictness ladder are the same tradeoff wearing three different names
because: Each replaces a single binary version-surface with a graduated axis specifically to avoid forcing every consumer onto the same all-or-nothing cutover: Stripe trades a growing internal shim chain for consumers who never face a hard migration deadline, AIP's channel/release/visibility axis trades more maintained surfaces for more predictable early-consumer guarantees, and Buf's FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE ladder trades looser enforcement for tolerating renames and file moves — all three answer 'how much internal complexity will we absorb to shrink the version-surface we expose.'

members.subject: Buf's four breaking-change strictness categories: FILE, PACKAGE, WIRE, WIRE_JSON
members.description: Which category an organization enforces is a governance decision with different blast radii: FILE catches source-level breakage that would fail a compile in strict languages like C++ or Python, while WIRE only cares whether bytes on the wire still decode correctly, tolerating renames and file moves that would break generated code. Choosing a looser category than your actual consumers need is a decision whose cost surfaces later, when a change Buf approved as 'non-breaking' still breaks a consumer that depended on generated-code stability Buf wasn't checking for.

members.subject: Buf breaking change detection quickstart
members.description: Confirmed by opening the page directly. Three progressive, concrete exercises against a real example repo (buf.build/tutorials/breaking): (1) local git comparison — add a new enum value and run detection against uncommitted changes; (2) BSR module comparison — rename an enum value (`PET_TYPE_HAMSTER` to `PET_TYPE_RODENT`), which buf correctly flags as breaking with the exact message shown on the page; (3) remote git comparison — move an enum into a new file and discover this breaks under the default FILE ruleset but not under the looser PACKAGE ruleset, directly demonstrating the strictness-ladder concept (FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE_JSON/WIRE) rather than just asserting it. Squarely in scope for schema-evolution/breaking-change governance practice.

members.subject: Google AIP stability-level strategies: channel-, release-, and visibility-based
members.description: Choosing among these is a judgment call with different long-term costs: channel-based is Google's recommended default because it avoids proliferating short-lived version identifiers, release-based gives more predictability to specific cohorts of early consumers at the cost of more surfaces to maintain, and visibility-based avoids new version identifiers entirely but requires access-control infrastructure. The wrong choice doesn't fail on day one - it shows up as either channel churn, or too many concurrently-supported pre-release surfaces, months into the API's life.

members.subject: Date-based API versioning as a governance model
members.description: Stripe's own engineering blog (opened directly) explains why they rejected major-version-number versioning: 'changes between versions being so big and so impactful for users that it's almost as painful as re-integrating from scratch,' and that scheme also forces a binary choice of freezing consumers on an old major version or cutting them off. Instead, Stripe pins every account to the API version active when it was created (a date, e.g. 2024-04-10); every incoming request for an older-pinned account is passed through a chain of small, per-change version-shim modules so that the internal service logic only ever has to implement the current schema, not a matrix of if/else branches for every historical version. This is a genuine judgment-level tradeoff: it adds real internal maintenance cost (an ever-growing chain of shims) in exchange for never forcing a disruptive re-integration on consumers, and is presented as a deliberate alternative to both URI-path and header-based major versioning.

members.subject: No-versioning / continuous compatible-evolution strategy (Stripe's rolling dates)
members.description: Per Stripe's own versioning writeup, a new account is automatically pinned to the latest version on its first API call; it keeps working on that version indefinitely unless the developer explicitly upgrades (via the dashboard) or overrides per-request with a Stripe-Version header. Each dated version bundles a small set of changes rather than a large breaking rewrite, so upgrades are incremental rather than all-or-nothing. Choosing this strategy versus versioned major releases is a governance decision: it demands building and maintaining a per-version compatibility-transform layer (see the companion mechanism row on Stripe's transformer architecture) in exchange for consumers never facing a hard cutover deadline.

members.subject: Stripe's version-transformer chain architecture
members.description: This is mechanism-level knowledge: it doesn't change how any single API call behaves in the normal case (a developer calling a pinned version just gets that version's shape, which is operation-level to use), but it explains behavior you can't predict without having seen the internals - for instance, why a single conceptual field change might appear at a different position or format depending on how many version-transform steps a given dated version sits behind current, or why Stripe's core business logic stays free of accumulated if/else version checks despite supporting essentially every version issued since 2011.

principle: Reproducible builds require pinning at three independent layers, each covering exactly what the others don't
because: The dependency lock file remembers provider version decisions, and is committed so those decisions go through review, but it explicitly never remembers module version decisions — which is the reason the module version argument can't be skipped just because a lock file exists — and required_version is a third, outermost layer pinning the CLI itself; a team that fails to move all three layers together doesn't get a clean one-line upgrade, it gets blocked mid-rollout by an unrelated module several layers down still pinned to the old constraint.

members.subject: Dependency lock file remembers provider version decisions
members.description: After Terraform selects a specific version for each provider dependency, it records that decision in a dependency lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) so that, by default, future `terraform init` runs reselect the same version instead of drifting to a newer one automatically.

members.subject: Commit the lock file so dependency changes go through code review
members.description: HashiCorp recommends committing the dependency lock file to version control specifically so that changes to external provider dependencies are visible and discussable in code review, the same way changes to configuration itself are reviewed — a direct lever for plan/apply review discipline at team scale.

members.subject: The dependency lock file never locks module versions
members.description: The dependency lock file tracks only provider dependencies. Terraform does not remember version selections for remote modules at all; on every init it reselects the newest available module version that satisfies the stated constraint. A team that commits .terraform.lock.hcl and concludes it now has reproducible builds is half right: providers are pinned, modules are not, and an unpinned or loosely-pinned module source will silently change between a plan run on a developer's machine and an init in CI with the identical committed lock file. This is the exact reason the module version argument (T3-058) cannot be skipped just because the lock file is committed.

members.subject: Pin external module versions with the version argument
members.description: HashiCorp recommends explicitly constraining the acceptable version numbers of every external module call, to avoid unexpected or unwanted changes. The same page states the version argument is only usable when the module's source points to a registry (the public Terraform Registry or a private registry); local-path modules do not support it because they share their caller's version, and for other source types (notably git) the pin has to be expressed in the source string itself. This is the second of the three pinning levels a team needs and is not covered by any provider-level mechanism.

members.subject: required_version pins the Terraform CLI version for a configuration
members.description: The terraform block's required_version setting specifies which versions of the Terraform CLI are allowed to run the configuration, and Terraform prints an error and exits without taking any action when the running CLI does not satisfy the constraint. This is the third and outermost level of version pinning at team scale -- distinct from provider constraints and from the dependency lock file, which the same docs note applies only to the CLI itself and not to provider plugins. Without it, engineers and CI runners on different CLI versions can produce different plans and, worse, a newer CLI can write a state format an older CLI cannot read.

members.subject: Provider/Terraform version bumps cascade through every module
members.description: Because each module pins or inherits its own required_providers and required_version constraints, upgrading the Terraform CLI or a provider version for a team's codebase means walking every module that uses it and bumping its constraint too - teams that treat this as a one-line change get blocked mid-upgrade by a module several layers down still pinned to the old version.

members.subject: Drill: intentionally break and repair a multi-module provider-version upgrade
members.description: In a repo with at least two modules that each declare their own required_providers constraints, bump the provider version constraint in only the root module and run `terraform init` — observe it fail or resolve inconsistently because the child modules are still pinned to the old constraint (T3-032). Commit the resulting `.terraform.lock.hcl` change and practice reading a lock-file diff the way a PR reviewer would (T3-018, T3-019). Then correctly walk every module, bump each constraint in turn, and re-run `init` to confirm the lock file re-resolves cleanly across the whole tree.

principle: CLI workspaces share one backend, so they cannot substitute for real environment isolation
because: That CLI workspaces multiplex several states under a single configuration is precisely the design fact that makes them unable to give different environments separate credentials or access controls, and HashiCorp's recommended fix — separate configurations per environment sharing logic through modules — only makes sense once the mechanism and its limitation are seen as cause and effect rather than two independent claims about workspaces.

members.subject: Static provider credentials are a risk even with rotation
members.description: HCP Terraform's own docs frame static credentials as a security risk in themselves, not just a risk when unrotated — the guidance explicitly states rotating static credentials regularly does not eliminate the risk, which is the stated motivation for using OIDC-based dynamic credentials instead. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-041 ("OIDC/dynamic credentials vs. static long-lived credentials"), which cited the identical quote. See merge log.]

members.subject: Terraform Associate practice exercises (state, modules, meta-arguments)
members.description: A third-party GitHub Pages set of six hands-on exercises for Terraform Associate prep covering AWS/GCP: first configuration, variables/outputs, resource dependencies, working with state (remote state and state locking), modules (creation/versioning/registry), and meta-arguments (count, for_each, lifecycle, dynamic blocks). Each exercise directory includes a README and a working solution.

members.subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Authenticate providers with dynamic credentials
members.description: Official hands-on tutorial that has the reader establish a trust relationship between HCP Terraform and a cloud provider, then configure a workspace to receive short-lived, run-scoped credentials via OIDC instead of static access keys.

members.subject: Saved plan files store sensitive data in cleartext
members.description: A saved Terraform plan file contains the full configuration, all planned values, and all plan options including input variables. If any of that data is sensitive — even if Terraform obscures it in terminal output — it is written to the plan file in cleartext, so saved plan files must be handled as sensitive artifacts (e.g., in CI/CD storage or artifact caches). [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: what a reader loses without this row is the knowledge that CI artifact retention is an access-control decision -- a choice made once whose failure is invisible at the moment it's made and surfaces only when the artifact store is later read by someone who shouldn't have access. That is judgment's late-surfacing signature, not operation's immediate one. Applied for consistency with T3-003, which Stage 2 already moved to judgment on the identical reasoning (Terraform writes secrets in cleartext, so control access to it).]

principle: A read_committed consumer isn't buffering or filtering messages itself -- it is gating delivery on control markers the transaction coordinator writes to the partition, and that single mechanism explains three separate symptoms
because: The coordinator writing a COMMIT or ABORT marker to every participating partition is what produces the offset gaps a naive consecutive-offset check would misread as loss, what makes a hung transaction able to stall consumption indefinitely until transaction.timeout.ms forces it closed, and what makes read_committed leave ordinary non-transactional writes completely untouched, since markers only exist where a transaction touched the partition.

members.subject: Transaction coordinator, transaction log, and commit/abort markers
members.description: KIP-98 describes the three components that make multi-partition atomicity possible: applications need 'the ability to write to several TopicPartitions atomically... either all messages are committed, or none of them are.' Each transactional producer connects to a transaction coordinator, a broker role that assigns PIDs, tracks transaction state, and drives commit/abort. The transaction log is an internal Kafka topic that durably persists this metadata so in-flight transactions can be recovered after a coordinator failure. When the producer calls commitTransaction() or abortTransaction(), the coordinator writes a COMMIT or ABORT marker as a control message to every partition that participated in the transaction; consumers use these markers to decide whether to surface or discard the transactional messages that preceded them.

members.subject: isolation.level: read_committed vs read_uncommitted, and offset gaps from control messages
members.description: The javadoc states that in read_committed mode 'the consumer will read only those transactional messages which have been successfully committed. It will continue to read non-transactional messages as before.' Internally this works via the Last Stable Offset (LSO): a read_committed consumer will not deliver messages past the LSO until it knows their transaction's outcome. The javadoc warns of a specific, easy-to-misdiagnose behavior: 'partitions with transactional messages will include commit or abort markers... applications reading from topics with transactional messages will see gaps in the consumed offsets' -- so code that assumes consecutive offsets (e.g. to detect missing messages) will misfire on any topic that uses transactions, even without message loss. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Summary states read_committed makes the consumer 'buffer and skip' aborted-transaction messages. The cited javadoc says verbatim: 'There is no client-side buffering in read_committed mode.' Summary also attributes marker-induced offset gaps to read_committed, where the javadoc says markers 'are filtered out for consumers in both isolation levels.' The row's own description is accurate; only the summary is wrong.]

members.subject: transaction.timeout.ms bounds how long an open transaction can block consumers
members.description: Documented as 'the maximum amount of time in milliseconds that a transaction will remain open before the coordinator proactively aborts it,' with a default of 60000ms. This setting is not just a producer-side cleanup knob: because read_committed consumers buffer transactional messages until they see the transaction's outcome marker, an abnormally long-lived open transaction directly stalls downstream consumption. transaction.timeout.ms is the backstop that guarantees a hung or crashed transactional producer cannot block read_committed consumers indefinitely.

members.subject: read_committed does not mean 'only transactional records'
members.description: isolation.level controls how a consumer treats transactional writes: read_uncommitted (the default) returns every record including ones from transactions that later abort, while read_committed withholds records from a transaction until it commits (using the Last Stable Offset as the visibility boundary) and drops records from aborted transactions entirely. The trap is assuming read_committed changes what non-transactional writes are visible -- it does not; ordinary produce calls outside any transaction are always visible immediately regardless of isolation.level. This matters for the exactly-once contract: a consumer must explicitly set isolation.level=read_committed to get end-to-end transactional semantics, since the client default is read_uncommitted, so a pipeline that enables producer transactions but forgets to set the consumer's isolation level will still see uncommitted/aborted data.

members.subject: Confluent Apache Kafka Internal Architecture -- Hands On: Transactions
members.description: From Confluent's 'Apache Kafka Internal Architecture' course. The reader provisions a Confluent Cloud cluster with Java client credentials, examines a transactional producer that initializes a transactional.id, sends 5 events under one transaction, and either commits or times it out. The core exercise: run a console consumer with isolation.level=read_committed and observe that it only surfaces the transactional events after the commit control message is written (contrasted against the Confluent Cloud Console UI, which uses read_uncommitted and shows messages immediately). A second part has the reader wait past the transaction timeout, trigger an expected producer exception, and confirm the read_committed consumer correctly ignores the aborted messages. Confirmed live and working when fetched, with concrete steps covering isolation levels, commit/abort, and consumer visibility.

principle: Dynamic credentials are a provider-agnostic trust exchange, not an HCP Terraform feature
because: That rotating static credentials doesn't remove their risk only becomes actionable once the actual replacement mechanism is shown in full: a signed identity token generated per run, verified against a public key, exchanged for temporary credentials, and discarded when the run ends. The connection this chapter surfaces is that this exact generate-verify-exchange-discard sequence is not proprietary to HCP Terraform — GitHub Actions implements the identical pattern for any CI runner — which no single row states on its own.

members.subject: Static provider credentials are a risk even with rotation
members.description: HCP Terraform's own docs frame static credentials as a security risk in themselves, not just a risk when unrotated — the guidance explicitly states rotating static credentials regularly does not eliminate the risk, which is the stated motivation for using OIDC-based dynamic credentials instead. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-041 ("OIDC/dynamic credentials vs. static long-lived credentials"), which cited the identical quote. See merge log.]

members.subject: OIDC workload identity token generation
members.description: For dynamic provider credentials, HCP Terraform itself generates a workload identity token that conforms to the OpenID Connect (OIDC) standard and embeds metadata about the organization, workspace or Stack, and run stage — this token, not a stored secret, is what gets presented to the cloud platform to authenticate a run.

members.subject: Successful OIDC verification yields temporary credentials
members.description: After the cloud platform verifies the workload identity token against HCP Terraform's public signing key, it responds by returning a set of freshly generated temporary credentials for that run to use — no long-lived secret is ever provisioned into the run.

members.subject: Temporary OIDC credentials are discarded when the run ends
members.description: Once a plan or apply run completes, HCP Terraform tears down the run environment and discards the temporary credentials that were issued for it, so no reusable long-lived credential persists after the run finishes.

members.subject: OIDC to a cloud provider is available in ordinary CI, not only HCP Terraform
members.description: All six OIDC rows in this set (T3-024 through T3-027, T3-041, T3-047) describe HCP Terraform's dynamic provider credentials, which leaves a reader with the false impression that the alternative to static keys is a HashiCorp product. The same trust exchange is available to a plain CI runner: GitHub Actions workflows can access cloud resources without storing any credentials as long-lived GitHub secrets, by requesting a signed OIDC token from GitHub, presenting it to the cloud provider, and receiving a short-lived access token scoped to that job run. For a team running Terraform in GitHub Actions against an S3 or GCS backend -- the most common non-HCP setup -- this, not HCP Terraform, is how the judgment in T3-024 actually gets implemented.

members.subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Authenticate providers with dynamic credentials
members.description: Official hands-on tutorial that has the reader establish a trust relationship between HCP Terraform and a cloud provider, then configure a workspace to receive short-lived, run-scoped credentials via OIDC instead of static access keys.

principle: A module built as a stable interface for a consumer who never opens its internals
because: Dependency inversion (T-012) and preconditions (T-013) exist so a module's consumer never has to open its internals to know what it needs or assumes; flat trees and shallow nesting (T-011, T-016) keep that contract traceable instead of buried in a chain; scoping by encapsulation, privilege, and volatility (T-015) draws the boundary so the interface doesn't leak scope it shouldn't; data-only modules (T-014) and shipping underspecified-but-over-exposed (T-017) are the same idea applied to reads and outputs; T-042 and T-049 are what building and then deliberately breaking that contract look like in practice.

members.subject: Automating Terraform plan/apply with GitHub Actions
members.description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Automate Terraform with GitHub Actions.' Sets up an HCP Terraform team token, workspace, and a template GitHub repo, then builds a plan workflow that runs on pull requests (uploads a speculative/read-only plan and comments the output on the PR) and an apply workflow that runs on pushes to main. Uses a stored HCP Terraform API token (TF_API_TOKEN, a GitHub Actions secret) for authentication rather than OIDC - useful as a plan-on-PR/apply-on-merge review-discipline exercise, but not an OIDC example.

members.subject: Multi-account/environment split strategy
members.description: For teams scaling Terraform usage, HashiCorp suggests splitting managed resources into multiple accounts in a way that makes organizational sense, giving the example of 'an account per deployment environment,' as one strategy alongside single-cloud, hybrid, or multi-cloud boundaries.

members.subject: VCS-driven speculative plans for PR review
members.description: As part of HashiCorp's recommended collaboration workflow, HCP Terraform's VCS integration generates speculative plans for each pull request, showing the exact changes Terraform will make, so teams can review infrastructure changes before they are merged/applied. This is presented as the review layer that sits above remote state and locking in the progression toward team collaboration. [AUDIT: the speculative-plan claim is verbatim-supported, but the closing sentence ('the review layer that sits above remote state and locking in a progression') is the harvester's framing, not the source's -- the page lists remote state, code review, and CI/CD as parallel practices, not a layered progression (Prohibition 2).]

members.subject: Running apply without a pre-generated plan file
members.description: Running terraform apply directly, without first saving and applying a specific plan file, lets Terraform generate a new plan at apply time, which can differ from whatever was reviewed, because time passes between review and execution during which real infrastructure or configuration may change. The described discipline is to plan to a file, review that exact plan, then apply that file rather than re-planning at apply time. [Stage 2: merged into T-007 (harvest-canon, 'Speculative plan staleness before apply') as a duplicate - same subject (plan/apply time-gap risk) and same depth (judgment); both recommend committing to one saved plan file and re-checking it rather than letting apply re-plan.] [AUDIT merged->viable (restored): Stage 2 incorrectly merged this row into T-007 as a duplicate. T-007's source says to re-check the final non-speculative plan before applying; this row's source says a saved plan file is applied exactly, with no re-planning. Different sources, near-opposite prescriptions -- not a duplicate. Restored to viable.]

members.subject: Treating a clean plan as a guarantee the apply will succeed
members.description: The same practitioner GitHub issue states: 'You assume that if you do a terraform apply, it will work. But more often than not, when you actually do the terraform apply, it errors out' - because a plan is computed against the provider's current view of things, and by apply time, provider-side state, quotas, or dependent resources can have changed, or the provider API can reject a change the plan predicted would succeed.

members.subject: Assuming Terraform detects drift automatically
members.description: A long-time Terraform user's GitHub issue lists 'no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation' as a core operational gap: detecting drift requires manually running terraform plan (or -refresh-only), and 'automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable' when configuration is complex. Terraform does not watch infrastructure and flag changes on its own - someone or something has to run a plan for drift to surface at all. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the second quoted phrase is not a quotation. The row presents "automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable" in quotation marks as source text; the GitHub issue (hashicorp/terraform#31736) instead says 'You cannot reliably implement a cron job, because a lot of times an automatic Terraform apply can fail.' A paraphrase presented as a quotation, with a substituted rationale ('when configuration is complex' vs. the source's 'an automatic Terraform apply can fail'). The first quoted phrase ('no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation') is verbatim-correct and the headline claim stands.]

members.subject: What a Terraform backend is
members.description: A backend defines where Terraform stores its state data files. The docs state: 'The backend defines where Terraform stores its state data files.' Backends allow state to be centrally stored so multiple team members can access and collaborate on the same infrastructure, rather than each person holding a local state file.

members.subject: Speculative plan staleness before apply
members.description: When using speculative plans (not saved to a file), the docs warn: 'other changes made to the target system in the meantime might cause the final effect of a configuration change to be different than what an earlier speculative plan indicated, so you should always re-check the final non-speculative plan before applying.' This is a stated limitation of plan review in team/CI workflows where time elapses between plan and apply. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Stage 2 merged T-036 into this row and appended a claim -- 'both recommend committing to one saved plan file rather than re-planning at apply time' -- that this row's own source (developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan) never states; that page's advice is to re-check the final plan, not to freeze one. T-036's source makes the opposite-facing recommendation (apply exactly the saved file, no re-planning). These are two distinct, source-grounded claims in real tension with each other -- the tension itself is a real team-scale plan/apply discipline question -- so the merge was incorrect and has been reversed; T-036 is restored to viable as its own row. See T-036.]

members.subject: Backend state key collisions across environments
members.description: Copying a dev directory to stand up staging without updating the backend's state key left both environments writing to the same state file. Applying staging caused Terraform to diff staging's desired config against the shared state (which reflected prod), and it began reconciling by modifying prod resources to match staging's configuration. Recovery took about 4 hours: using CloudTrail to determine which resources belonged to which environment, manually importing them into separate state files, then re-applying to correct drift.

principle: The same portability that lets a CI plan file cross machines is what exposes it in cleartext
because: T-020's requirement that plan and apply run as separate CI steps sharing one archived working directory is what forces the plan to persist to disk between stages at all; T-021 shows credentials can be kept off disk via env vars, but T-056 shows the plan file itself cannot be - HashiCorp states outright that any sensitive data in a plan is saved in cleartext, so the same split that makes review and portability possible is what turns the artifact into a wider-audience leak.

members.subject: CI pipeline: separate plan/apply steps and plan-file portability constraints
members.description: HashiCorp's automation tutorial recommends running init, plan, and apply as distinct steps (terraform init -input=false; terraform plan -out=tfplan -input=false; terraform apply -input=false tfplan). After plan, the entire working directory including .terraform must be archived and made available to the apply step, and both steps must run on the identical absolute path, operating system, and CPU architecture, since 'Terraform assumes that the plan will be applied on the same operating system and CPU architecture as where it was created.'

members.subject: CI credential handling and PR secret exposure risk
members.description: The tutorial recommends using environment variables for provider authentication credentials rather than persisting them to disk, since env vars 'are not included in the plan or persisted to disk by Terraform in any other way.' It separately warns that 'passing sensitive/secret data to Terraform via variables or via environment variables will make it possible for anyone who can submit a PR to discover those values' in pull-request-triggered plan workflows.

members.subject: Saved plan files are sensitive artifacts
members.description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- absent from the harvested/merged set. The plan/apply-review cluster (T-007, T-020, T-021, T-036) tells a team to write plans to a file with -out and to archive the working directory between CI stages, and none of those rows say what the plan file contains. principle: The partition, not the topic, is Kafka's atomic unit of ordering, isolation, and sequencing
because: Partition-to-consumer exclusivity, the assign() API's bypass of group coordination, a poison pill stalling exactly one partition rather than the whole topic, and the idempotent producer's per-(PID, partition) sequence counter are all expressions of a single design fact: Kafka assigns ownership, sequences writes, and isolates failure at the partition boundary, never at the topic or the consumer boundary.

members.subject: Partition-to-consumer exclusivity
members.description: The javadoc states the assignment invariant directly: 'if there is a topic with four partitions, and a consumer group with two processes, each process would consume from two partitions.' This exclusivity is what gives Kafka in-order, non-duplicated delivery per partition within a group -- two members of the same group never read the same partition concurrently. It also caps useful parallelism: a group cannot usefully have more active consumers than the topic has partitions, because the excess consumers will be assigned zero partitions.

members.subject: Manual partition assignment bypasses group coordination
members.description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc documents assign() as an alternate, lower-level API: it 'disables dynamic partition assignment and consumer group coordination.' A consumer using assign() specifies its partitions directly and does not participate in rebalances, heartbeats, or the group protocol at all -- it is not a member of a consumer group in the coordination sense even if group.id is set. This matters operationally because none of the rebalance-related configuration (session.timeout.ms, ConsumerRebalanceListener, static membership, cooperative assignors) applies to assign()-based consumers.

members.subject: Poison pill messages block the whole partition
members.description: When a consumer's deserializer cannot parse a record (commonly because a producer changed serialization format, or the consumer is configured with the wrong key/value deserializer), the default behavior is that the exception is thrown before the offset for that record is ever advanced. Because the consumer re-polls and hits the same record again, it enters an infinite retry loop against that one 'poison pill' message, and every other message queued behind it on that partition is starved indefinitely -- this is not a whole-consumer crash, it is a silent partition-level stall that can go unnoticed until lag alarms fire. Confluent's own guidance is to never let deserialization exceptions propagate up to block re-polling; the documented fix (for the Java/Spring stack) is a wrapping ErrorHandlingDeserializer that catches the failure, returns null plus a DeserializationException header, and routes the record to a dead-letter topic via a recoverer, which lets the offset advance past the bad record.

members.subject: Idempotent producer: producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers
members.description: KIP-98 introduces the mechanism behind enable.idempotence: each producer session gets a unique PID transparently at initialization. For every (PID, TopicPartition) pair the producer maintains a sequence number starting at zero and incrementing by one per message. The broker validates that an incoming message's sequence number is exactly one greater than the last one it committed for that (PID, partition); a duplicate (already-seen) sequence number is silently deduplicated, while a gap (a sequence number skipping ahead) is treated as a fatal error signaling data loss. This is what converts producer-retry-driven duplication -- previously an unavoidable side effect of at-least-once retries -- into effectively-exactly-once writes for a single producer session, without requiring the application to dedupe anything itself.

members.subject: Re-derive why a poison pill stalls one partition and not the topic
members.description: Reason from the single-integer-offset model rather than from a remembered answer. Then list the exits (skip, dead-letter topic, retry with backoff) and name the guarantee each one costs you.

principle: Everything about how a consumer group divides and reassigns work is downstream of one invariant: a partition is owned by exactly one member of a group at a time
because: That single exclusivity rule is what makes scaling past partition count a wasted consumer, what per-topic assignor math can turn into a lopsided split across multiple topics, and what a reader has to run forward by hand to predict correctly under churn; assign() is included as the boundary case, since it is the literal switch that turns this entire coordinated-division apparatus off for a given consumer.

members.subject: Consumer group membership
members.description: All KafkaConsumer instances that share the same group.id belong to one consumer group. Kafka's broker-side group coordination automatically balances the partitions of subscribed topics among the live members of the group, so a group functions as a single logical subscriber even though it is made of many processes. This is the mechanism that lets consumption scale horizontally: adding more consumer processes to the same group.id increases parallelism without any application-level coordination code.

members.subject: Partition-to-consumer exclusivity
members.description: The javadoc states the assignment invariant directly: 'if there is a topic with four partitions, and a consumer group with two processes, each process would consume from two partitions.' This exclusivity is what gives Kafka in-order, non-duplicated delivery per partition within a group -- two members of the same group never read the same partition concurrently. It also caps useful parallelism: a group cannot usefully have more active consumers than the topic has partitions, because the excess consumers will be assigned zero partitions.

members.subject: Partition count is the ceiling on group parallelism, and ordering is per-partition
members.description: Two consequences of the one-partition-to-one-consumer rule that the row set states nowhere, both in canon the run already opened. On parallelism, the KafkaConsumer javadoc says of the one-consumer-per-thread model: 'The number of total threads across all processes will be limited by the total number of partitions.' A group with more members than the topic has partitions leaves the extras assigned nothing; scaling a consumer group past the partition count buys zero throughput, and the only remedy is adding partitions (which is itself not free -- the 4.3 consumer-configs page warns that 'altering partition numbers while setting this config to latest may cause message delivery loss'). On ordering, the design page says the topic 'is divided into a set of totally ordered partitions, each of which is consumed by exactly one consumer within each subscribing consumer group at any given time' -- total order holds inside a partition and nowhere else, so any cross-partition sequencing a reader assumes is unfounded, and the message key (which selects the partition) is what actually buys ordering for a given entity. Added by audit: K-004 states the exclusivity rule but neither of these consequences, and both are load-bearing for reading K-014, K-043 and K-054 correctly.

members.subject: partition.assignment.strategy default list
members.description: partition.assignment.strategy is documented as 'a list of class names or class types...of supported partition assignment strategies,' with the current default value being the pair RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor. Because it is a list, the client and every other group member negotiate down to the first strategy in the list that all members mutually support; this is how a fleet can be rolled from one assignor to another (e.g. migrating toward cooperative rebalancing per KIP-429) without a hard cutover -- during the transition window, members advertise both and the group converges on whichever both the old and new members share.

members.subject: RangeAssignor can produce lopsided assignment across multiple topics
members.description: RangeAssignor lays out each topic's partitions in numeric order and the group's consumers in lexicographic order, then divides partition count by consumer count per topic -- consumers early in that ordering get any remainder partitions. Because this is done independently per topic rather than globally, a consumer subscribed to multiple topics can end up with a disproportionately large share of total partitions: the documented example is 2 topics x 4 partitions with 3 consumers, where consumer 1 gets 4 partitions (one extra from each topic) while consumers 2 and 3 get 2 each. This is a decision people get wrong by assuming 'range' means an even split -- it only guarantees an even split within a single topic, and the imbalance compounds with topic count. Kafka's default assignment strategy since 2.4+ is CooperativeStickyAssignor, which does not have this per-topic stacking behavior, but RangeAssignor remains available and is still explicitly configured in some codebases.

members.subject: Predict rebalance behavior before running it
members.description: Pick concrete numbers (for example 3 consumers, 8 partitions). Predict the assignment under RangeAssignor and under CooperativeStickyAssignor. Then predict what changes when a fourth consumer joins, when one is SIGKILLed, and when one blocks for longer than max.poll.interval.ms. Check the last case against what the coordinator actually does, since it differs from the first two.

members.subject: Confluent Apache Kafka 101 -- Hands-on Exercise: Kafka Consumer
members.description: Part of Confluent's free Apache Kafka 101 course. The reader signs up for a Confluent Cloud cluster, sets up a Python virtual environment and the confluent-kafka client library, configures real connection credentials, and writes a working consumer script with group.id=python_kafka101_group_1 and auto.offset.reset=earliest so it reads from the start of a topic with no committed offsets. The consumer polls in a loop and handles graceful disconnection. Confirmed live and working when fetched: it is a concrete, executable exercise (not just narrative documentation), and it exercises consumer groups, offset management, and partition assignment through the group mechanism.

principle: A module's reusability comes from a boundary drawn on purpose, not an accretion of resources
because: Being single-purpose and opinionated is not a vague ideal — the encapsulation/privilege/volatility criteria give it operational teeth as three independent cuts on the same boundary decision, and the thin-wrapper anti-pattern shows what happens when that boundary is drawn so small it stops abstracting anything at all: a failure in the opposite direction from a sprawling module, but of the identical boundary-setting judgment, which only becomes visible by holding all three claims together.

members.subject: Modules should be opinionated and single-purpose
members.description: HashiCorp's module-creation pattern guidance says a good module does one thing well and is deliberately opinionated; if you struggle to explain what a module's purpose is, that itself signals the module has taken on too much complexity to be reusable.

members.subject: Module scoping: encapsulation, privilege, volatility
members.description: HashiCorp names three specific considerations for scoping a module for reuse: group infrastructure that is always deployed together (encapsulation), restrict a module to a single privilege boundary, and separate long-lived infrastructure from short-lived infrastructure (volatility) rather than mixing them in one module.

members.subject: Avoid thin-wrapper modules; raise the abstraction level
members.description: A well-designed module should introduce a new concept in your architecture built out of underlying provider resource types, rather than being a thin wrapper around a single resource type that adds no real abstraction.

members.subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Module creation - recommended pattern
members.description: Official hands-on HashiCorp tutorial that walks through scoping a three-tier web application into six separate reusable modules (network, web, app, database, routing, security), applying encapsulation/privilege/volatility criteria to decide module boundaries, then documenting them for other teams to consume.

principle: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire, not by name, and that single fact generates its entire safety discipline
because: Numbers being the actual wire identity is why reuse silently corrupts data instead of erroring, why deletion requires reservation rather than plain removal, why the wire-safe/unsafe tiering exists as a lookup table keyed to that same wire behavior, and why marking a field required creates a one-way commitment no future version can retract; the compare-drill only resolves once a reader can state that Avro matches by name and Protobuf by number.

members.subject: NONE compatibility mode disables schema safety checks
members.description: This is a judgment-level trap-adjacent concept: choosing NONE removes the registry's only automated safety net, and the consequence (a deserialization failure in production) surfaces later, at read time on whichever consumer first encounters the incompatible data, not at schema-registration time. It's sometimes a legitimate choice (e.g. during early prototyping, or for topics with a single tightly-coupled producer/consumer pair deployed atomically) but the decision to use it needs to be deliberate, not a default left unconfigured.

members.subject: Buf breaking change detection quickstart
members.description: Confirmed by opening the page directly. Three progressive, concrete exercises against a real example repo (buf.build/tutorials/breaking): (1) local git comparison — add a new enum value and run detection against uncommitted changes; (2) BSR module comparison — rename an enum value (`PET_TYPE_HAMSTER` to `PET_TYPE_RODENT`), which buf correctly flags as breaking with the exact message shown on the page; (3) remote git comparison — move an enum into a new file and discover this breaks under the default FILE ruleset but not under the looser PACKAGE ruleset, directly demonstrating the strictness-ladder concept (FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE_JSON/WIRE) rather than just asserting it. Squarely in scope for schema-evolution/breaking-change governance practice.

members.subject: Schema Registry's default compatibility mode is BACKWARD
members.description: Confluent's schema-evolution documentation states that 'the default compatibility mode is BACKWARD', checked non-transitively against the latest registered version only. This matters more than a default usually does, because BACKWARD is not a neutral setting: per the same page it permits adding optional fields and removing fields, and it fixes the rollout order -- consumers upgrade before producers. A team that never touches the compatibility configuration has therefore made a governance decision (A-033) without knowing it, and will find out at the first rollout where a producer ships first. It also explains a common surprise: a schema change rejected by a registry nobody configured is being rejected by BACKWARD's rules specifically, not by generic 'schema validation'. Added by audit: six rows in this set discuss selecting among the modes (A-001, A-022, A-025, A-033, A-043, A-045) and none states which one applies by default.

members.subject: Deprecation and Sunset link relations for policy documentation
members.description: The header alone only carries a date; the link relation is how a provider attaches an explanation. Zalando's own deprecation guidance builds on the same pattern, requiring producers to add a description explaining the deprecation and provide a migration manual - the RFC-level link relation is the standard mechanism for surfacing exactly that kind of documentation to automated clients rather than only humans reading changelogs.

members.subject: Protobuf field numbers are permanent wire identifiers
members.description: This is the single most load-bearing operation-level rule in Protobuf schema evolution: field names can be freely changed (they don't appear on the wire at all, only in generated source), but field numbers are the actual identity of a field to any decoder, old or new. Violating it doesn't produce a compile error - it silently corrupts data at runtime, which is exactly the kind of immediate-but-easy-to-miss failure that defines the operation tier.

members.subject: Draft a deprecation timeline with every required signal
members.description: Produce the actual timeline with dates. Include the Deprecation and Sunset headers with correct relative ordering, the link relation to the policy document, the notice window and your justification for its length, and how you determine whether every affected consumer has migrated. Then answer whether you may shut down without their consent, and what your answer depends on.

principle: Two independent gates inserted at the same seam between plan and apply, one human and one machine
because: T-022's VCS-triggered speculative plan and T-026's policy-as-code evaluation are structurally the same move performed by different actors: both intercept a run at the identical seam between plan and apply rather than changing what plan or apply compute, one requiring a human reviewer to read the diff and the other requiring an automated policy set to pass before the run is allowed to continue.

members.subject: VCS-driven speculative plans for PR review
members.description: As part of HashiCorp's recommended collaboration workflow, HCP Terraform's VCS integration generates speculative plans for each pull request, showing the exact changes Terraform will make, so teams can review infrastructure changes before they are merged/applied. This is presented as the review layer that sits above remote state and locking in the progression toward team collaboration. [AUDIT: the speculative-plan claim is verbatim-supported, but the closing sentence ('the review layer that sits above remote state and locking in a progression') is the harvester's framing, not the source's -- the page lists remote state, code review, and CI/CD as parallel practices, not a layered progression (Prohibition 2).]

members.subject: Policy-as-code position in the plan/apply pipeline
members.description: In HCP Terraform, for each run in selected workspaces, the platform checks the Terraform plan against the configured policy set - policy evaluation happens during planning, before apply. Depending on enforcement level, failed policies can stop the run. Users with appropriate permissions can override failed policies. HashiCorp recommends storing policies in version control for 'standardization, security, and auditability.' [AUDIT depth judgment->operation: the depth_check as harvested justified judgment by pointing at a decision ('choosing enforcement levels and who may override') the row's own content does not actually teach.]

principle: At-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once are not three settings to pick between; they are one axis -- when the offset commit happens relative to processing -- read at different points
because: Whether a crash produces loss or a duplicate is decided entirely by which side of the processing step the commit lands on, so auto-commit's fixed timer losing unprocessed records, a manual commit racing a side effect that already fired, and the fact that even disciplined manual commit ordering can't close the duplicate window are the same mechanism observed from three different failure angles, not three unrelated bugs.

members.subject: Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once
members.description: Per the official design documentation: at-most-once means messages may be lost but are never redelivered, achieved by committing offsets before processing completes. At-least-once means messages are never lost but may be redelivered -- this is the default behavior when offsets are committed after processing. Exactly-once means each message is processed exactly once; the docs state this requires 'coordinating the consumer's position with what is actually stored as output,' which in practice means using a transactional producer together with a read_committed consumer. These are not consumer-only settings -- the achieved semantic is a joint property of producer config (acks, idempotence, transactions) and consumer config (commit timing, isolation.level).

members.subject: Auto-commit timing window
members.description: A widely repeated mistake is assuming auto-commit means 'Kafka safely tracks my progress for me.' In practice, the automatic commit fires on the next call to poll() and commits the offsets returned by the previous poll() -- it is decoupled from whether the consumer actually finished processing those records. If the consumer crashes after poll() returns a batch but before it finishes handling all records in that batch, the next commit (on the following poll or the commit interval, default 5s via auto.commit.interval.ms) may commit offsets past records that were never fully processed, silently dropping them from the at-least-once guarantee people assume auto-commit provides. A related, separately documented race: calling pause() during graceful shutdown while auto-commit is on can seek to stale cached offsets and overwrite correct committed offsets, causing already-processed messages to be reprocessed on restart. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Origin https://github.com/confluentinc/confluent-kafka-javascript/issues/404 is a client-library bug report: pause() seeks to a stale #lastConsumedOffsets entry and commits it immediately under enable.auto.commit=true. That is not the general 'auto-commit commits the offset from the last poll(), not the batch just processed' mechanism the row asserts. Related phenomenon, wrong mechanism. Repoint origin to the KafkaConsumer javadoc, which does support the claim.]

members.subject: enable.auto.commit and its data-loss risk
members.description: enable.auto.commit defaults to true, with auto.commit.interval.ms defaulting to 5000ms, meaning offsets are committed roughly every 5 seconds regardless of processing progress. The javadoc warns explicitly: 'if you fail to [consume all data before subsequent calls or closing], it is possible for the committed offset to get ahead of the consumed position, which results in missing records' -- i.e. records can be silently skipped on the next restart if the consumer crashes after an auto-commit but before finishing processing of the corresponding batch. This is a judgment call the docs surface directly: auto-commit is simple and adequate when occasional message loss on crash is acceptable, but manual commit is required when correctness demands at-least-once processing.

members.subject: At-least-once still requires an idempotent consumer, even with careful commit ordering
members.description: The standard at-least-once recipe is enable.auto.commit=false plus a manual commit issued only after the consumer has fully processed a batch's side effects. This closes the message-loss failure mode of auto-commit (never marking a message done before it's actually done) but does not and cannot close the duplicate-processing failure mode: if the process crashes or is rebalanced away after the side effect (e.g. a DB write or downstream publish) succeeds but before the offset commit is acknowledged, the next owner of that partition will start from the last committed offset and reprocess the already-applied message. This is why every at-least-once consumer that has externally visible side effects needs its own idempotency mechanism (dedup key, upsert semantics, idempotent API call) independent of anything Kafka's client does -- the guarantee Kafka gives is about redelivery, not about effects. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Origin https://tarkalabs.com/blogs/kafka-message-duplication/ describes duplicates arising from a poll-timeout eviction and rebalance ('Kafka will assume that the service is dead... the same message will then be assigned to, and processed by, another consumer in the group'), not from 'a crash between finishing processing and committing the offset' as the row asserts. The conclusion (at-least-once needs an idempotent consumer) is right and the article does present that solution; the stated mechanism is not the cited one.]

members.subject: Trace the loss and duplicate windows for each commit strategy
members.description: Write out a three-column table: auto-commit, sync-commit-after-process, sync-commit-before-process. For each, mark the instant a crash produces loss and the instant it produces a duplicate. The exercise is done when you can state which strategy gives at-most-once and which gives at-least-once without looking it up, and can point at the line of code where the window opens.

principle: Whether an additive change is safe is not a property of the wire format — it is conditional on the consumer choosing to be a tolerant reader
because: Every claim in this set that adding a field is 'safe' or 'not breaking' (Graph's catalogue, JSON Schema's open model) is quietly assuming a lenient consumer; the identical change is breaking under a strict/closed-model reader or a real strict-parsing mobile client, so the safety verdict tracks the consumer's leniency, not the change itself.

members.subject: Definition of a breaking change (Microsoft REST API Guidelines)
members.description: This is orientation-level: without this definition a reader cannot correctly classify any specific change as breaking or safe, which blocks everything downstream (versioning, deprecation, governance). Concrete examples the guidelines list as breaking: removing or renaming APIs or parameters, behavioral changes to existing APIs, changes to error codes and fault contracts, and anything that violates the 'principle of least astonishment.' The guidelines flag that even additive changes like new JSON response fields can break naive clients that do strict schema validation, which is why they insist each service publish its own explicit definition rather than relying on a universal one.

members.subject: Microsoft Graph's catalogue of breaking vs. non-breaking changes
members.description: Graph's own working definition: 'any change that requires a client to change its implementation to continue working with the service.' This catalogue operationalizes that definition into a checklist a reviewer can apply directly to a proposed change, which is what distinguishes it from the orientation-level definition alone - this is the concrete list you apply correctly in the normal case, and getting an item wrong (e.g. treating a non-nullable property addition as safe) breaks clients immediately upon deployment.

members.subject: JSON Schema's open vs. closed content model and its effect on compatibility
members.description: This is a schema-design judgment call specific to JSON Schema among the three serialization formats: an open model is more forgiving of producer-side additions (new fields simply pass through undeclared) but weaker at catching typos or unintended extra data; a closed model is stricter and catches those, but a producer that adds any new field without updating the reader schema will have every message rejected outright. The consequence of the wrong choice doesn't appear until the first field addition under a closed model, or the first unwanted-data leak under an open one - both late-surfacing costs typical of judgment-level knowledge.

members.subject: Adding a response field is always safe
members.description: A first-hand account (a team's own postmortem-style writeup) describes pushing what they believed was a purely additive JSON response change; three mobile apps crashed because they used strict JSON parsers that rejected the unexpected new field. The general pattern behind this trap: 'additive' is a schema-level judgment, but real consumers include code paths (strict deserializers, typed clients, PUT-based updates that round-trip and re-send a payload, systems with fixed-width storage columns) that are broken by fields they didn't ask for. The corrective framing from the same body of writing: treat additions as low-risk, not risk-free, and gate them behind the same contract-testing/consumer-visibility discipline as other changes rather than skipping review because 'it's just additive.'

members.subject: Triage a change list into breaking, non-breaking, and depends-on-consumer
members.description: Write ten changes: add optional response field, add required request field, remove an enum value, widen an int to a long, rename a field, tighten validation, change a default, reorder an array, add an error code, change a timeout. Sort into breaking, non-breaking, and depends. The third pile is the real exercise, and the consumer assumption that decides it is the thing worth being able to say out loud.

members.subject: The tolerant reader: consumers must accept compatible extensions
members.description: Zalando's compatibility chapter carries the rule '{MUST} prepare clients to accept compatible API extensions', instructing that 'service clients should apply the robustness principle' and specifically 'be tolerant with unknown fields in the payload', citing Fowler's TolerantReader and the ACM piece 'The Robustness Principle Reconsidered'. This is the hinge the rest of the topic hangs on. Every claim in this row set that an additive change is non-breaking -- Microsoft Graph's 'adding new elements is allowed and is not considered a breaking change' (A-016), Protobuf's 'adding new fields is safe' (A-044), Avro's writer-field-ignored rule (A-008), Schema Registry's BACKWARD mode permitting added fields (A-022) -- is conditional on the consumer being a tolerant reader. It is also the direct explanation of the A-048 trap: adding a response field is safe against a tolerant reader and breaks a strict-parsing or round-tripping client, which is exactly why Microsoft's guidelines require each service to publish its own definition of breaking (A-002). Choosing a strict parser is a decision whose cost lands late, on someone else's compatible deploy. Added by audit: the run opened this file twice (A-004, A-047) and took the versioning sections roughly ninety lines below this rule without taking the rule, leaving the topic's entire consumer-side obligation unrepresented across 59 API rows.
