because: Whether a crash produces loss or a duplicate is decided entirely by which side of the processing step the commit lands on, so auto-commit's fixed timer losing unprocessed records, a manual commit racing a side effect that already fired, and the fact that even disciplined manual commit ordering can't close the duplicate window are the same mechanism observed from three different failure angles, not three unrelated bugs.

members.subject: Decoupling consumption from processing via a worker thread pool
members.description: The javadoc's recommended pattern for handling slow or variable-latency processing: 'move message processing to another thread, which allows the consumer to continue calling poll while the processor is still working,' combined with disabling automatic commits and manually committing 'processed offsets for records only after the thread has finished handling them.' This is presented as a choice among two documented multi-threading patterns -- one-consumer-per-thread (simplest, 'often the fastest', but uses more TCP connections) versus decoupled consumption/processing (a single consumer feeding a thread pool via a blocking queue, which 'allows independently scaling the number of consumers and processors' but requires careful coordination so offsets are only committed for fully-processed records).

members.subject: Choosing commitSync vs commitAsync is a throughput/safety tradeoff, not a correctness switch
members.description: commitSync() blocks the polling thread until the broker acknowledges the commit, and it will automatically retry on retriable errors -- this is reliable but forces the consumer loop to pay a network round-trip and reduces throughput. commitAsync() does not block and optionally takes a callback for success/failure, which is faster under load, but a failed async commit is not automatically retried by the client, and because commits can be reordered, blindly retrying a stale async commit risk overwriting a later, valid commit with an older offset. The judgment call practitioners have to make deliberately: use commitAsync() in the steady-state poll loop for throughput, but call commitSync() on rebalance (in the revoke callback) and on shutdown, where a blocking guarantee actually matters and there's no 'next commit' to fall back on.

members.subject: Transaction coordinator, transaction log, and commit/abort markers
members.description: KIP-98 describes the three components that make multi-partition atomicity possible: applications need 'the ability to write to several TopicPartitions atomically... either all messages are committed, or none of them are.' Each transactional producer connects to a transaction coordinator, a broker role that assigns PIDs, tracks transaction state, and drives commit/abort. The transaction log is an internal Kafka topic that durably persists this metadata so in-flight transactions can be recovered after a coordinator failure. When the producer calls commitTransaction() or abortTransaction(), the coordinator writes a COMMIT or ABORT marker as a control message to every partition that participated in the transaction; consumers use these markers to decide whether to surface or discard the transactional messages that preceded them.

members.subject: Idempotent producer scope
members.description: The idempotent producer assigns each producer instance a unique Producer ID (PID) plus a per-partition monotonically increasing sequence number; the broker only accepts a write whose sequence number is exactly one greater than the last accepted one for that (PID, partition) pair, which rejects duplicate retries. The trap: this state is scoped to a single producer session and a single partition. If the producer application restarts, it is issued a new PID and sequence numbers reset to zero -- so duplicates are possible across restarts even with idempotence enabled. It also does nothing about duplicates already present in the data the producer read from its own source (e.g. a duplicate read from an upstream system); Kafka cannot deduplicate what the producer already sent it twice.

members.subject: acks controls producer durability with a latency/durability tradeoff
members.description: The producer configuration docs describe three acks levels: 0 (fire-and-forget, no server ack), 1 (wait for the leader broker's ack only -- can lose data if the leader fails before followers replicate), and all (wait for acknowledgment from every in-sync replica, the strongest durability guarantee Kafka offers at the producer level). The current documented default is 'all'. The docs state a hard constraint, not just a recommendation: 'enabling idempotence requires this config value to be all' -- so a producer that wants exactly-once-style deduplication cannot trade away durability by lowering acks. This is presented as a genuine choice for producers not using idempotence: acks=1 is faster but can silently lose the most recent unreplicated write on leader failure; acks=all is slower but survives leader failure as long as one in-sync replica is alive.

principle: Environment identity is never self-verifying, whether it's a workspace selector or a copied backend key
because: T-009 and T-010 establish that CLI workspaces share one backend and one set of credentials with no directory-level signal of which is selected; T-003 is the mechanism (partial backend configuration) that lets directories avoid that by giving each environment its own backend config; T-030 and T-032 are incidents on each side of that same failure mode - an invisible workspace selector and a copied backend key that was never updated - showing directories are the recommended fix (T-031) but not an automatic one; T-051 drills both failure modes side by side.

members.subject: Backend configuration syntax and partial configuration
members.description: A configuration can only provide one backend block, and a backend block cannot refer to named values like input variables, locals, or data source attributes. You do not need to specify every required argument in the backend block itself - missing values can be supplied via a config file with -backend-config=PATH, command-line key/value pairs with -backend-config="KEY=VALUE", or interactive prompts during init. This is the mechanism teams use to keep per-environment backend settings out of shared configuration.

members.subject: CLI workspaces: state-per-workspace mechanics
members.description: The persistent data in a backend belongs to a workspace; a backend initially has only one workspace ('default', which cannot be deleted) containing one state. Multiple workspaces let you deploy distinct instances of the same configuration without configuring a new backend or changing credentials. Terraform does not access resources in other workspaces when you switch - they still physically exist but are invisible until you switch back.

members.subject: CLI workspace selection before apply
members.description: A team running environments as Terraform CLI workspaces had an engineer apply without checking which workspace was selected; production instances scaled down to the dev instance count (2 instead of 20), a production incident lasting 15 minutes and affecting 200+ users. The practitioner attributes this to workspaces making the active environment implicit - the same command applies to whichever workspace is currently selected, with no directory-level signal of which environment is being touched.

members.subject: Workspaces vs. directories for environment separation
members.description: HashiCorp explicitly states CLI workspaces are not appropriate when organizations want strong separation between deployment stages (e.g. staging/production) that need different credentials and access controls, because 'CLI workspaces within a working directory use the same backend, so they are not a suitable isolation mechanism for this scenario.' The recommended alternative is separate configurations (directories) that each instantiate reusable modules against a different backend, so each environment gets its own backend config and credentials.

members.subject: Choosing Terraform CLI workspaces vs. directory-per-environment
members.description: A practitioner who migrated a team from CLI workspaces to per-environment directories reports the workspace setup accumulated conditionals keyed on `terraform.workspace` (e.g. `contains(["prod","staging","staging-eu","staging-special"], terraform.workspace)`) that became hard to audit, and that after migrating to folders 'code reviews went from mental workspace simulation to reading 50 lines of actual config,' with no further wrong-environment incidents. Their stated default is per-environment folders for teams under 25 engineers and up to 12 environments, prioritizing explicit configuration over the DRY-ness of workspaces. [Stage 2: considered as a possible duplicate of T-010 (harvest-canon, 'Workspaces vs. directories for environment separation') - same subject and same depth, but not merged: T-010's claim is HashiCorp's stated reason (credential/access-control separation), while this row's claim is a practitioner's distinct reasons (unauditable per-workspace conditionals, code-review cost) plus a concrete team-size/environment-count threshold not present in T-010. Kept as two rows carrying different supporting evidence for a related recommendation.]

members.subject: Backend state key collisions across environments
members.description: Copying a dev directory to stand up staging without updating the backend's state key left both environments writing to the same state file. Applying staging caused Terraform to diff staging's desired config against the shared state (which reflected prod), and it began reconciling by modifying prod resources to match staging's configuration. Recovery took about 4 hours: using CloudTrail to determine which resources belonged to which environment, manually importing them into separate state files, then re-applying to correct drift.

members.subject: Drill: workspaces-vs-directories migration
members.description: Build a two-environment (dev/prod) setup using Terraform CLI workspaces against one backend, sized so that `terraform.workspace` gates at least one differing value (e.g. instance count). Deliberately reproduce T-030's failure mode: switch to the dev workspace, then run apply while believing you are targeting prod, and observe how little signal there is that you are in the wrong workspace. Then refactor into two separate directories, each with its own backend configuration and credentials, re-run the same change, and write down at what team size or environment count (compare your answer to T-031's stated threshold) you would judge the workspace approach acceptable versus not.

principle: Rows that did not resolve into a shared principle
because: These did not group under any binding idea I could name. fetch.min.bytes is a genuine throughput/latency tunable in this topic, but nothing else in this row set shares its mechanism (broker-side fetch-response batching) closely enough to bind it to a principle rather than a category. Kept here as lookup rather than reading.

members.subject: fetch.min.bytes trades latency for throughput/efficiency
members.description: Documented as 'the minimum amount of data the server should return for a fetch request,' with a default of 1 byte -- meaning by default the broker returns data as soon as any is available, prioritizing low latency. Raising fetch.min.bytes (paired with fetch.max.wait.ms as the latency cap) causes the broker to wait for more data to accumulate before responding, which reduces the number of fetch round-trips and request overhead per byte transferred, at the direct cost of added end-to-end latency for low-throughput partitions. This is a standard throughput-vs-latency dial the docs present as a tunable rather than a fixed correctness setting.

principle: Drift detection is nothing more than a scheduled plan, implemented differently with and without HCP Terraform
because: Defining drift detection as periodic, non-actionable refresh-only plans is what resolves the scheduling question of what happens when a real run starts mid-assessment: the assessment gets cancelled rather than the run, because it was only ever a plan competing for the same lock, not a privileged process. The open-source equivalent, an exit-code contract a team's own cron job parses instead of a scheduled product feature, is the same underlying mechanism wearing a different interface — a connection invisible if the HCP-only rows are read without the non-HCP one.

members.subject: Drift detection runs as periodic refresh-only plans
members.description: HCP Terraform's drift detection works by determining whether real-world infrastructure still matches the Terraform configuration, implemented as periodic health assessments that run non-actionable, refresh-only plans against the workspace's tracked state without changing infrastructure or state themselves. [VERIFY gap, caught by 3B in passing / missed by 3A: the stored quote ("Drift detection determines whether your real-world infrastructure matches your Terraform configuration") supports only the row's first clause. The mechanism detail appended to it -- "implemented as periodic health assessments that run non-actionable, refresh-only plans against the workspace's tracked state without changing infrastructure or state themselves" -- is not in the stored quote and was not independently verified this stage. Recorded as a real gap in the Haiku verify pass: a partial quote that only covers the easy half of a two-clause claim.]

members.subject: Health assessments never interrupt an active run
members.description: HCP Terraform's automated health assessments (which power drift detection) are designed to never block or interfere with a real plan/apply run — if a new run starts while an assessment is in progress, HCP Terraform cancels the assessment rather than the run.

members.subject: Drift detection without HCP Terraform: plan -detailed-exitcode
members.description: Every drift-detection row in this set (T3-008, T3-028) describes HCP Terraform health assessments, which a team not on HCP Terraform cannot use. The open-source equivalent is terraform plan -detailed-exitcode, which changes the command's exit codes so a scheduled job can distinguish outcomes programmatically: 0 means succeeded with an empty diff, 1 means error, and 2 means succeeded with a non-empty diff, i.e. drift or pending changes. Exit code 2 is what a cron job or CI schedule alerts on. Without this, a scripted drift check has to parse human-readable plan output, which is not a stable interface.

members.subject: Drill: manually induce and detect infrastructure drift
members.description: Apply a small Terraform-managed resource, then modify it out-of-band — through the cloud console or CLI, not through Terraform — so its real state diverges from configuration. Run `terraform plan` and confirm it correctly reports the drift as a diff to reconcile (T3-028). If using HCP Terraform, configure a scheduled health assessment on the workspace, trigger a run while an assessment happens to be in progress, and confirm the assessment is what gets cancelled, not the run (T3-008) — the non-obvious ordering the drift-detection docs specify.

principle: The lock file's reproducibility guarantee stops at the provider boundary and never reaches modules
because: T-053 establishes that a committed lock file makes provider version resolution durable and identical across every machine that runs init; T-054 shows that same guarantee was never extended to modules - Terraform will always resolve the newest module version matching a constraint, with no lock file involvement at all - so a team that trusts the committed lock file to have frozen 'the dependency set' has left one entire class of dependency unpinned without knowing it.

members.subject: The dependency lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl)
members.description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- absent from the harvested/merged set; no row mentions the lock file, required_providers, or version pinning of any kind. terraform init creates and updates .terraform.lock.hcl, which 'belongs to the configuration as a whole, rather than to each separate module.' HashiCorp's instruction is explicit: 'You should include this file in your version control repository so that you can discuss potential changes to your external dependencies via code review, just as you would discuss potential changes to your configuration itself.' Once a provider selection is recorded, init reuses that exact version 'even if a newer version has become available'; terraform init -upgrade is what 'disregard[s] the existing selections and once again select[s] the newest available version matching the version constraint.' Without a committed lock file, two engineers and CI can each resolve a different provider version from the same configuration and produce three different plans from identical code -- the single most direct way a team loses plan reproducibility.

members.subject: The lock file does not lock module versions
members.description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- absent from the harvested/merged set. The dependency lock file covers providers only. HashiCorp: 'At present, the dependency lock file tracks only provider dependencies. Terraform does not remember version selections for remote modules, and so Terraform will always select the newest available module version that meets the specified version constraints.' The trap is assuming committing .terraform.lock.hcl froze the whole dependency set. It did not: a registry module without a version constraint silently upgrades on the next init, on whichever machine inits next. The module block's version argument is the only guard, and HashiCorp recommends 'explicitly constraining the acceptable version numbers to avoid unexpected or unwanted changes' -- but that argument is available only 'when the source argument points to a module listed in a registry', so a team sourcing modules from raw Git URLs has no version argument at all and must pin via the source ref itself. This is the unstated condition underneath the module-reuse cluster (T-011 through T-017): that guidance assumes consumers can pin what they consume, and nothing else in the set says how.

principle: Modules are wired together by composition, and breaking that contract breaks callability
because: Composition — a module receiving its dependencies as inputs rather than creating its own copies — is the mechanism that makes a flat, shallow module tree achievable instead of deep nesting, with the two-level rule as its concrete numeric form; the shared-provider-block failure is that mechanism's breakage made visible, since a module that embeds its own provider configuration has made something global that composition requires to be parameterizable, which is exactly why Terraform then refuses to let it be called with count, for_each, or depends_on.

members.subject: Composition: modules receive dependencies rather than embedding them
members.description: In the composition pattern, a module does not create and manage its own private copy of a dependency; instead it receives that dependency as an input from the root module. This is what lets the same root module wire the same child modules together differently to produce different systems.

members.subject: Keep the module tree flat; prefer composition over deep nesting
members.description: HashiCorp's module development guidance recommends keeping the overall module tree relatively flat and using module composition — combining sibling modules at the root rather than nesting modules inside modules — because flat, composed modules are easier to reuse in different combinations.

members.subject: Limit primary module nesting to two levels deep
members.description: As a general rule, primary modules should not be nested more than two levels deep, with an explicit exception carved out for small, common utility modules such as ones that just apply tags. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: the row's own depth_check names the consequence as 'module trees that are hard to reuse' -- a cost realized later, the judgment signature, not operation's 'breaks immediately and visibly.' A four-deep module tree plans and applies fine. Inconsistent as operation with sibling row T3-017 (thin-wrapper modules), which makes the same class of claim and is correctly judgment.]

members.subject: A shared module with its own provider block can't be called with count/for_each/depends_on
members.description: A module meant to be called by other modules must not define its own provider blocks; if it does, Terraform rejects using that module call with the for_each, count, or depends_on meta-arguments, because provider configurations are global to the whole configuration and can't be parameterized per-instance the way those arguments imply.

members.subject: Drill: refactor a mega-module into scoped, composed modules
members.description: Take a single flat root configuration that manages several unrelated pieces of infrastructure as one module (e.g. a VPC, a compute service, and a database). Split it into separate modules scoped by HashiCorp's own encapsulation, privilege, and volatility criteria (T3-013); wire them together via composition, with the root module passing outputs as inputs rather than any module embedding its own provider or a dependency it doesn't own (T3-016); keep nesting to no more than two levels (T3-014); and audit the result for thin-wrapper modules — any module that is just one resource with no real abstraction — eliminating or merging them (T3-017).

principle: Where the version identifier lives — URL path, query string, or content-negotiation header — decides what a future change gets coupled to
because: Path versioning couples the version to the URL itself and to gateway routing, so migrating consumers means changing every call site and every co-located service must agree on one mechanism; query-string versioning is only safe once path stability is already guaranteed; header/media-type versioning decouples the version from the URL at the cost of a pastable link — three schemes solving the same problem by choosing a different thing to couple the version to, which is why no scheme is actually free.

members.subject: REST versioning strategy: URI path segment
members.description: Both the Microsoft REST API Guidelines and Google's AIP-185 describe URI-path versioning as a first-class option: the version appears as a leading path segment (Microsoft: /v1.0/products; Google: the major version is the first path component, e.g. /v1/). Microsoft's guideline requires that 'services co-located behind a DNS endpoint MUST use the same versioning mechanism' so that a single gateway can route consistently. Google AIP-185 additionally requires pre-stable versions to suffix the stability level onto the version segment (v1beta, v1alpha) while stable versions carry no suffix. The tradeoff versus header/media-type schemes: URI versioning is transparent and cache-friendly but couples the URL itself to the version, so migrating consumers means changing every call site. [AUDIT viable->wounded: 'the most common versioning scheme', 'cache-friendly' and 'routable by gateways' appear in NEITHER cited source. Microsoft's Guidelines.md presents path versioning as one of two options with the rule 'Services that cannot ensure URL path stability across future versions MUST embed the version in the URL path'; it never characterises it that way. The description also attributes the co-location MUST to gateway routing, whereas the document's stated reason is 'a consistent user experience across the endpoint is paramount.' Relabel the rationale as interpretation.]

members.subject: REST versioning strategy: query-string parameter
members.description: Guidelines.md section 12 presents query-string versioning (https://api.contoso.com/products/users?api-version=1.0) alongside URI-path versioning as the two primary schemes, plus an optional date-grouped variant (YYYY-MM-DD) that maps internally to Major.Minor. The guide is explicit about when each applies: 'Services guaranteeing URL path stability across versions may adopt query strings; services unable to ensure path stability must embed versions in the URI path.' This makes the choice conditional on an operational guarantee, not a stylistic preference.

members.subject: REST versioning strategy: media-type (Content-Type) versioning
members.description: The Zalando compatibility chapter states the rule as a MUST: a major version number embedded in the path (e.g. /v1/customers) is disallowed because it creates 'tighter coupling and complexer release management' between provider and consumer release cycles. The mandated alternative is media-type versioning via HTTP content negotiation: the version travels in the Content-Type header as a parameter on a custom media type, e.g. application/x.<custom-media-type>+json;version=<version>. Zalando frames this as a last resort, though: the guidelines' stronger preference is to avoid versioning altogether by evolving the API through backward-compatible extensions, and to version only when a compatible extension is impossible.

members.subject: Zalando's rejection of URL versioning as a governance decision
members.description: This is a judgment-level example precisely because it contradicts the majority convention (used by Stripe, GitHub, and most public APIs per URI-path). Zalando's compatibility.adoc argues that a version number in the path forces every consumer to coordinate a URL change with every provider release, and that this coupling is worse than the added complexity of content-negotiation-based media types. The consequence of choosing wrongly is not visible immediately - both schemes 'work' on day one - it shows up later as either painful multi-version URL sprawl (URI scheme at scale) or brittle content-negotiation tooling and debugging friction (media-type scheme at scale).

members.subject: Consistent versioning mechanism required across co-located services
members.description: Guidelines.md states this as a MUST-level rule under the versioning section. Mixing schemes behind one endpoint breaks routing assumptions immediately and visibly - a gateway configured to parse path-segment versions will silently mis-route (or fail to route) a request that instead carries its version in a query string, and vice versa. This is a correctness rule for using the chosen scheme, not a strategy choice itself. [AUDIT viable->wounded: The MUST-level rule is real and quoted correctly ('Services co-located behind a DNS endpoint MUST use the same versioning mechanism'), but the stated reason -- 'because a gateway or client library cannot correctly dispatch a mix' and 'a gateway configured to parse path-segment versions will silently mis-route' -- is not the document's rationale. Guidelines.md gives 'a consistent user experience across the endpoint is paramount.' Unsupported mechanism attached to a supported rule, labeled cited fact.]

members.subject: Major.Minor version numbering convention
members.description: Guidelines.md ties the numbering scheme directly to the breaking-change definition elsewhere in the same document: a breaking change requires a major-version bump, while backward-compatible additions may use a minor-version bump. This gives consumers a mechanical way to know, from the number alone, whether an upgrade requires code changes.

members.subject: Google AIP: APIs must not expose minor or patch version numbers
members.description: This is stricter than Microsoft's Major.Minor convention: Google's model treats every non-breaking change as an in-place update to the same major version, so minor/patch numbers would be meaningless noise to the consumer. The rule is specifically about what appears in the interface surface (package name, URI path), not about internal build or release tracking.

members.subject: URI-path versioning has no cost
members.description: Troy Hunt's long-running, widely-referenced piece on API versioning argues against the idea that any one versioning mechanism is simple or costless. He makes the semantic case against URI versioning directly: 'URLs suck [as a versioning mechanism] because they should represent the entity' — the resource is the same resource regardless of representation version, so baking version into the URI conflates identity with representation. He also concedes the practical case for it (shareable, clickable, cache-friendly URLs) but is explicit that the header/Accept-based alternative has its own real cost (you lose a pastable URL; clients must construct requests carefully). His conclusion is not 'URI versioning is right' or 'wrong' but that teams treating their chosen scheme as free of tradeoffs, in either direction, are wrong — 'None of these are bad in any tangible sense... they're just different.' The trap is skipping the tradeoff analysis because URI versioning looks like the default, low-effort choice.

principle: Every constraint enable.idempotence enforces on other producer settings is a direct requirement of the PID-plus-sequence-number check the broker actually runs, and that same check draws the boundary on what idempotence can and can't deduplicate
because: The broker only accepts a write whose sequence number is exactly one more than the last one it saw for that (PID, partition) pair, which is why in-flight requests must stay boundable, why retries must stay on, and why acks=all is non-negotiable -- the ack has to reflect the write the sequence check just validated; the same per-session, per-partition scope is also why a producer restart resets the count and reopens the door to cross-restart duplicates idempotence was never meant to catch.

members.subject: enable.idempotence config and its enforced constraints
members.description: enable.idempotence is documented as: 'when set to true, the producer will ensure that exactly one copy of each message is written in the stream.' Kafka does not let this be enabled in isolation -- it enforces (or auto-corrects) three other settings: max.in.flight.requests.per.connection must be at most 5 (idempotence needs the broker to see requests in an order it can validate sequence numbers against, which breaks down with unbounded in-flight requests), retries must be greater than 0 (idempotence exists specifically to make retries safe, so disabling retries defeats its purpose), and acks must be 'all' (idempotence's guarantee is only meaningful if the broker's ack reflects full replication). Since Kafka 3.0, enable.idempotence defaults to true, meaning these constraints are the default behavior unless a user explicitly reconfigures around them.

members.subject: Idempotent producer: producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers
members.description: KIP-98 introduces the mechanism behind enable.idempotence: each producer session gets a unique PID transparently at initialization. For every (PID, TopicPartition) pair the producer maintains a sequence number starting at zero and incrementing by one per message. The broker validates that an incoming message's sequence number is exactly one greater than the last one it committed for that (PID, partition); a duplicate (already-seen) sequence number is silently deduplicated, while a gap (a sequence number skipping ahead) is treated as a fatal error signaling data loss. This is what converts producer-retry-driven duplication -- previously an unavoidable side effect of at-least-once retries -- into effectively-exactly-once writes for a single producer session, without requiring the application to dedupe anything itself.

members.subject: Idempotent producer scope
members.description: The idempotent producer assigns each producer instance a unique Producer ID (PID) plus a per-partition monotonically increasing sequence number; the broker only accepts a write whose sequence number is exactly one greater than the last accepted one for that (PID, partition) pair, which rejects duplicate retries. The trap: this state is scoped to a single producer session and a single partition. If the producer application restarts, it is issued a new PID and sequence numbers reset to zero -- so duplicates are possible across restarts even with idempotence enabled. It also does nothing about duplicates already present in the data the producer read from its own source (e.g. a duplicate read from an upstream system); Kafka cannot deduplicate what the producer already sent it twice.

members.subject: acks controls producer durability with a latency/durability tradeoff
members.description: The producer configuration docs describe three acks levels: 0 (fire-and-forget, no server ack), 1 (wait for the leader broker's ack only -- can lose data if the leader fails before followers replicate), and all (wait for acknowledgment from every in-sync replica, the strongest durability guarantee Kafka offers at the producer level). The current documented default is 'all'. The docs state a hard constraint, not just a recommendation: 'enabling idempotence requires this config value to be all' -- so a producer that wants exactly-once-style deduplication cannot trade away durability by lowering acks. This is presented as a genuine choice for producers not using idempotence: acks=1 is faster but can silently lose the most recent unreplicated write on leader failure; acks=all is slower but survives leader failure as long as one in-sync replica is alive.

principle: Parallel execution is safe only because graph construction already resolved dependencies and cycles first
because: The 9-phase construction in T-027 adds nodes, wires depends_on and interpolation edges, and validates a single acyclic root before any walk begins; T-028's depth-first-with-parallelism traversal and its default concurrency of 10 are only correct because that validation already happened - the concurrency knob is safe to turn precisely because it operates on a graph whose ordering constraints were proven, not assumed.

members.subject: Configuration drift vs. state drift distinction
members.description: HCP Terraform's docs draw an explicit distinction: 'Configuration drift differs from state drift. Drift detection does not detect state drift.' Configuration drift is a mismatch between real infrastructure and the Terraform configuration; state drift involves external changes that don't necessarily invalidate configuration. When configuration drift is found, HCP Terraform proposes the changes needed to bring infrastructure back in sync with configuration.

members.subject: Configuring OIDC-based dynamic provider credentials
members.description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Authenticate providers with dynamic credentials.' Walks through setting up a trust relationship between HCP Terraform and a cloud provider via OIDC, running Terraform locally to establish the provider-specific trust configuration, setting workspace variables to enable dynamic credential requests, then provisioning infrastructure through HCP Terraform using the established trust. Covers AWS, GCP, Azure, and Vault, plus AWS EKS and GKE variants.

principle: State's dual nature: a shared source of truth that is also a plaintext-secret liability
because: State's binding function — it is the record of what already exists, consulted instead of re-inspecting real infrastructure on every run — is exactly why it must be both shared across the team and locked down: the same authoritative document that makes collaboration possible also stores every managed resource's secrets in plaintext, so remote storage and access restriction are not two separate best practices but two responses to one architectural fact about what state is.

members.subject: Purpose of Terraform state
members.description: Terraform state exists to bind objects that already exist in a remote system to the resource instances declared in configuration, so Terraform can determine what already exists without re-inspecting the real infrastructure on every run. This binding function is why state must be tracked accurately and shared across a team rather than reasoned about locally.

members.subject: Remote state for team collaboration
members.description: HashiCorp's own guidance is to store state in HCP Terraform or a remote backend rather than locally, specifically to secure it and allow team members to collaborate on the same infrastructure without passing state files around manually.

members.subject: State must not be stored in plain version control
members.description: Storing Terraform state in a version control system or any storage that lacks state locking and secure access control is explicitly discouraged, because it can cause data loss or expose secrets that end up embedded in the state file. [Stage 2 depth correction: reclassified from operation to judgment — see merge log.]

members.subject: State file contents are sensitive by default
members.description: Terraform's state file stores a JSON snapshot of every managed resource, including secrets, passwords, and other sensitive attribute values in plaintext, so it must be treated as sensitive data with restricted access and encrypted, versioned remote storage - not committed to source control or left world-readable in a bucket. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: identical reasoning to T3-022 and T3-003 -- three rows making one claim ('Terraform writes your secrets somewhere in cleartext, so control access to it') should not sit at two different depths. T3-003 was already moved to judgment by Stage 2 on this exact reasoning.]

principle: Secrets land in cleartext on disk regardless of the sensitive flag, in state and in saved plans alike
because: T-055 establishes that state stores real values in plaintext regardless of how they got there, and that marking a variable sensitive only hides it from terminal output while backend-specific encryption is what actually protects the file at rest; T-047's certification questions test the same fact directly (secrets referenced as variables end up in plaintext in state) - the 'sensitive' flag and backend encryption solve two different halves of the same leak, and testing on one doesn't confirm the other is in place.

members.subject: HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate sample questions
members.description: Official HashiCorp sample-questions page for the Terraform Associate (004) certification. Provides real example questions in the exam's three formats (true/false, multiple choice, multiple answer) covering topics including state file contents (e.g. that secrets referenced as variables end up in plain text in state), variable map syntax, automatic loading of terraform.tfvars, which commands refresh state, and what happens during apply. States explicitly: 'The exam questions are not intended to trick you.'

members.subject: State stores secrets in plaintext, so state access is an access-control decision
members.description: AUDIT DISCOVERY -- present in the merged set only as an incidental clause inside an exam-practice row (T-047) and a passing mention of the backend `encrypt` option inside a tutorial's steps (T-046); no row states it directly. HashiCorp: 'If you are developing with Terraform locally, Terraform stores your state in a plaintext file, which includes any secret values you defined in your configuration.' Marking a variable or output sensitive obscures terminal output; it does not keep the value out of state. Recommendations are backend-dependent and explicit: 'You can encrypt your state at rest, but the encryption method depends on your specific backend'; 'The S3 backend can encrypt state at rest if you enable the encrypt option, and protects state with TLS in transit'; 'HCP Terraform automatically encrypts state at rest and protects it with TLS in transit.' Alongside: 'Use access controls to limit who has access to your state' and 'Use audit logs to track state access over time.' At team scale this converts a storage choice into a permissions decision -- read access to the state bucket is read access to every credential any provider has ever returned.

principle: Locking guards against concurrent writers, not against a human confirming the wrong command
because: Locking (T-004) and its concrete backend implementation (T-046) exist to stop two processes writing state at once, not to stop a single confirmed destructive command; force-unlock (T-005) is the manual override for the first case, and T-029/T-048 show how that override becomes its own hazard once a human second-guesses it by hand; T-034 is the case where the team assumed Terraform's own protections would catch a wrong-context destroy and learned the protection that saved them lived in Azure, not Terraform.

members.subject: Automatic state locking on write operations
members.description: State locking happens automatically on all operations that could write state, with no message shown when it succeeds. If state locking fails, Terraform does not continue. Not all backends support locking, so the guarantee is backend-dependent. Most commands support a -lock=false flag to disable locking, which the docs advise against using.

members.subject: Setting up S3 remote state with DynamoDB locking, then migrating
members.description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Migrate state from S3 to HCP Terraform.' Has the reader create an S3 bucket and DynamoDB table for state storage and locking, deploy an EC2 instance against that backend, create CLI workspaces (default and dev), then replace the S3 backend configuration with HCP Terraform's cloud block, rename workspaces, assign a variable set with AWS credentials to the new workspaces, and run plan/apply remotely through HCP Terraform before cleaning up.

members.subject: force-unlock and the lock-ID nonce
members.description: When automatic unlocking fails, terraform force-unlock provides manual recovery, but the docs warn: 'Be very careful with this command. If you unlock the state when someone else is holding the lock it could cause multiple writers.' The command requires a unique lock ID that Terraform outputs only when unlocking fails, functioning as a nonce that ensures locks and unlocks target the correct lock rather than any lock.

members.subject: State locking and force-unlock
members.description: Terraform locks state automatically before any write operation; if state locking fails, Terraform does not continue. Teams hit this when a CI runner is killed mid-apply (OOM, timeout, spot termination) or someone Ctrl+C's a long-running apply, leaving a stale lock. principle: Consumer-driven contracts move authority over what counts as breaking from the provider to the consumer
because: Pact's testing workflow, the JS and JVM workshops that drill it hands-on, Fowler's account of consumer-driven contract ownership, and the caution against treating contract tests as integration coverage are all facets of the same authority shift: once a contract is generated from actual consumer usage rather than a provider-authored schema, the provider's freedom to change anything a consumer doesn't depend on becomes visible and enforceable before release, not after.

members.subject: Pact: consumer-driven contract testing workflow
members.description: This is orientation-level because it establishes what consumer-driven contract testing fundamentally is and how it differs from schema-first approaches: rather than a static schema describing every possible interaction, the contract is generated from the consumer's actual usage, so 'only parts of the communication that are actually used by the consumer(s) get tested.' members.subject: Consumer-driven contract ownership
members.description: Martin Fowler's original Consumer-Driven Contracts article (opened directly) describes the pattern as consumer contracts expressing consumer expectations, adopted by the provider so that 'consumer contracts effectively define which parts of that provider contract currently support the business value realized by the system.' This is a judgment-level design decision, not a mechanical testing choice: it determines who has authority over what counts as a breaking change. A provider-authored contract can change anything the provider didn't anticipate a consumer needing; a consumer-driven contract makes any change that breaks a registered consumer expectation visible before release, at the cost of providers now depending on consumers actually maintaining and publishing their contracts (typically via a broker).

members.subject: Contract tests as a substitute for integration tests
members.description: Microsoft's public Engineering Fundamentals Playbook, in its consumer-driven contract (CDC) testing chapter (opened directly), states: 'Contract tests are not the place to verify internal business logic and correctness of the consumer,' and cautions that CDC scope must be kept tight so it doesn't blur into 'other higher level functional testing layers.' The practical failure mode this guards against: a team adopts Pact-style contract tests, sees them pass, and treats that as equivalent coverage to a full integration or end-to-end suite — but contract tests only verify that a specific consumer-provider interaction matches an agreed shape; they say nothing about network behavior, infra, multi-service call sequencing, or a consumer's own business logic. Related literature (Martin Fowler's original Consumer-Driven Contracts article, opened directly) frames CDC instead as a design discipline: consumers author the contract to make the provider's evolution safe for them, which is a narrower and different goal than end-to-end verification.

principle: Kafka's exactly-once machinery only ever deduplicates a write to a Kafka partition, so the practical guarantee for any real pipeline is bounded by the last Kafka-internal write, and everything past that point falls back on the same idempotent-consumer discipline at-least-once always required
because: transactional.id is what makes a producer's identity durable across restarts so the boundary itself can be recovered and fenced, and the required producer-plus-consumer combination is what extends that boundary as far as the consumer's own commit -- but a database write, an API call, or any effect outside Kafka sits past the boundary regardless, which is the exact gap the two drills are built to make someone locate by hand rather than assume away.

members.subject: transactional.id enables cross-session recovery and zombie-producer fencing
members.description: The producer-configs docs describe transactional.id as enabling 'reliability semantics which span multiple producer sessions since it allows the client to guarantee that transactions using the same TransactionalId have been completed prior to starting any new transactions.' KIP-98 frames the underlying design tradeoff: a stable transactional.id lets the coordinator recognize when a new producer instance is restarting with the same identity as a previous one and needs to resolve that previous instance's dangling transaction before proceeding -- and it lets the coordinator bump an internal epoch to fence off ('zombie') the old instance if both are somehow still running, so an old, stale producer process cannot write into a transaction a newer instance has already taken over. This is a judgment call for operators: transactional.id must be assigned per logical producer identity (e.g. per partition-owning task), not shared across concurrently-running instances, or fencing will reject legitimate writers.

members.subject: End-to-end exactly-once requires a specific combination of producer and consumer settings together
members.description: The Kafka design documentation is explicit that 'achieving exactly-once requires: transactional producer with transactional.id set, plus consumer using isolation.level=read_committed and enable.auto.commit=false. This ensures atomicity across both production and offset tracking.' This is a judgment-level configuration decision because each piece is individually necessary but not sufficient: enabling idempotence alone only deduplicates a single producer's retries; enabling transactions alone without read_committed lets a downstream consumer see uncommitted (possibly-aborted) data; and auto-commit racing against transactional writes can commit consumer offsets independently of whether the corresponding output write actually committed, breaking the atomicity the whole scheme exists to provide.

members.subject: Scope of exactly-once semantics
members.description: The most common EOS misconception is treating it as an end-to-end guarantee: 'we're using Kafka with exactly-once semantics, so we don't have to worry about duplicates.' In reality Kafka's exactly-once (idempotent producer + transactions) only guarantees that writes to Kafka topics/partitions and Kafka Streams state are applied once. The moment a consumer does anything outside Kafka -- writes to a database, calls a REST API, publishes to another queue -- that write is outside the transaction boundary. If the consumer crashes after the external write but before committing its offset, the record is reprocessed on restart regardless of EOS being enabled upstream. The article's recommended defenses are idempotent consumer logic, the transactional outbox pattern, and offset-aware idempotency keys, not relying on Kafka EOS alone.

members.subject: Assemble the minimum config set for end-to-end exactly-once

members.subject: Classify a pipeline's real delivery guarantee end to end

members.subject: session.timeout.ms and heartbeat.interval.ms
members.description: session.timeout.ms is described as 'the timeout used to detect client failures when using Kafka's group management facility' -- if no heartbeat arrives within this window, the coordinator triggers a rebalance and gives the dead consumer's partitions to other members. heartbeat.interval.ms controls the frequency of the background heartbeat thread's pings to the coordinator. These two settings are broker-side-configurable defaults too (group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms / group.consumer.session.timeout.ms) with the same numeric defaults (5000ms / 45000ms) in the newer consumer group protocol. Lowering session.timeout.ms detects real failures faster but increases the odds of false-positive rebalances from transient GC pauses or network blips.

members.subject: max.poll.interval.ms and CommitFailedException
members.description: A very common production error is 'Commit cannot be completed since the group has already rebalanced and assigned the partitions to another member' (CommitFailedException). The instinctive read is a broker or network problem; the actual cause documented across support threads and blog postmortems is that the time between successive poll() calls exceeded max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes), because record processing inside the poll loop took too long. The coordinator has no other signal that a consumer is alive except calls to poll(), so it evicts the member and reassigns its partitions, and the pending commit is then rejected as coming from a member no longer in the group. The two accepted fixes are raising max.poll.interval.ms to match real processing time, or lowering max.poll.records so each batch finishes well inside the interval -- one case study reported an 80% drop in rebalances after cutting max.poll.records from 500 to 50.

members.subject: max.poll.interval.ms and the processing-time / liveness tradeoff
members.description: If poll() is not called again within max.poll.interval.ms, the javadoc states 'the client will proactively leave the group so that another consumer can take over its partitions,' which can surface to the application as a CommitFailedException on the next commit attempt. The docs explicitly name the failure mode: a consumer that keeps sending heartbeats (so it looks alive) but never calls poll() again because it is stuck processing is a 'livelock.' This makes max.poll.interval.ms a judgment call tied to worst-case processing latency per poll() batch, not a fixed operational constant -- setting it too low causes spurious rebalances under normal load spikes, too high delays detection of a truly stuck consumer.

members.subject: max.poll.records bounds work-per-poll but not time-per-poll
members.description: Documented as 'the maximum number of records returned in a single call to poll(),' defaulting to 500. This setting only bounds batch size, not wall-clock time: 500 records that each take 100ms to process would still take 50 seconds of processing, which could exceed max.poll.interval.ms if that is left at its default of 300000ms (5 min) or lower. The two settings are commonly confused because they both relate to the poll loop, but they answer different questions -- max.poll.records answers 'how much work can one poll() hand me,' max.poll.interval.ms answers 'how long do I have to finish that work before the group considers me dead.' Tuning one without the other is a common source of the livelock/rebalance failure mode described in the max.poll.interval.ms row.

members.subject: session.timeout.ms / heartbeat.interval.ms is a failure-detection-speed vs false-eviction tradeoff
members.description: session.timeout.ms (broker-side default 45s at the time reviewed) is how long the group coordinator waits without a heartbeat before declaring a member dead and triggering a rebalance; heartbeat.interval.ms (default 3s) is how often the client sends heartbeats, and is recommended at no more than 1/3 of session.timeout.ms so a few missed heartbeats don't immediately trip eviction. This is a judgment call, not a fixed-answer setting: a shorter session.timeout.ms detects genuinely crashed consumers faster (less downstream lag before another member takes over their partitions), but it also raises false-positive evictions during normal but momentarily slow behavior -- a GC pause, a slow disk flush, a brief CPU spike -- which then trigger a full rebalance for a consumer that was never actually dead.
