members.subject: Static membership (group.instance.id) trades faster restarts for slower failure detection
members.description: KIP-345 introduces group.instance.id as a stable, user-provided identifier that survives process restarts, replacing the ephemeral member.id normally regenerated on each join. When a static member restarts within the session timeout, the broker returns its cached assignment immediately with no group-wide rebalance -- this targets two use cases the KIP names directly: heavy stateful applications where rebalancing causes major performance degradation, and rolling deployments where each instance bounce would otherwise trigger a rebalance. The KIP is explicit about the cost: this design is 'prioritizing state persistence over liveness,' meaning a truly failed static member is not detected until session.timeout.ms expires rather than via an explicit leave-group signal (static members deliberately skip sending LeaveGroup on shutdown). The KIP recommends extending session timeouts to as much as 30 minutes for this pattern, and warns that duplicate group.instance.id values across consumers cause a FENCED_INSTANCE_ID error.

principle: Provider configuration is global to the whole run, and every constraint here follows from that fact
because: The dependency lock file pinning a version decision, the elevated risk assigned to static provider credentials, version bumps cascading through every module that declares its own required_providers, and the ban on count/for_each/depends_on for modules with their own provider block are all consequences of one rule: a provider configuration cannot be parameterized per module instance, because Terraform resolves providers once for the entire configuration rather than once per module.

members.subject: Dependency lock file remembers provider version decisions
members.description: After Terraform selects a specific version for each provider dependency, it records that decision in a dependency lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) so that, by default, future `terraform init` runs reselect the same version instead of drifting to a newer one automatically.

members.subject: Static provider credentials are a risk even with rotation
members.description: HCP Terraform's own docs frame static credentials as a security risk in themselves, not just a risk when unrotated — the guidance explicitly states rotating static credentials regularly does not eliminate the risk, which is the stated motivation for using OIDC-based dynamic credentials instead. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-041 ("OIDC/dynamic credentials vs. static long-lived credentials"), which cited the identical quote. See merge log.]

members.subject: Provider/Terraform version bumps cascade through every module
members.description: Because each module pins or inherits its own required_providers and required_version constraints, upgrading the Terraform CLI or a provider version for a team's codebase means walking every module that uses it and bumping its constraint too - teams that treat this as a one-line change get blocked mid-upgrade by a module several layers down still pinned to the old version.

members.subject: A shared module with its own provider block can't be called with count/for_each/depends_on
members.description: A module meant to be called by other modules must not define its own provider blocks; if it does, Terraform rejects using that module call with the for_each, count, or depends_on meta-arguments, because provider configurations are global to the whole configuration and can't be parameterized per-instance the way those arguments imply.

members.subject: Drill: intentionally break and repair a multi-module provider-version upgrade
members.description: In a repo with at least two modules that each declare their own required_providers constraints, bump the provider version constraint in only the root module and run `terraform init` — observe it fail or resolve inconsistently because the child modules are still pinned to the old constraint (T3-032). Commit the resulting `.terraform.lock.hcl` change and practice reading a lock-file diff the way a PR reviewer would (T3-018, T3-019). Then correctly walk every module, bump each constraint in turn, and re-run `init` to confirm the lock file re-resolves cleanly across the whole tree.

principle: The classic protocol's synchronous join/sync handshake is what makes a rebalance a full-group pause, not just a housekeeping event for the member that changed
because: The RPC design -- every member must rejoin, only the elected leader computes assignment, and a new generation ID invalidates anyone still on the old one -- is inherited from the earliest ZooKeeper-registration design and is the actual mechanism behind why any single trigger (a join, a leave, a topic change) stops every member in the group, not only the one whose membership changed.

members.subject: Original design: automatic consumer load balancing as the precursor to the modern group coordinator
members.description: The original design deck (Kreps, Narkhede, Rao; hosted on the Apache Kafka project wiki) shows 'Auto Consumer Load Balancing' as: brokers and consumers register in ZooKeeper, consumers listen to broker and consumer registration changes, and each such change triggers a consumer rebalance. This is architecturally distinct from the current protocol (a dedicated broker-side group coordinator driving JoinGroup/SyncGroup/Heartbeat, later evolving further under KIP-848 into fully server-computed assignment) but establishes the enduring shape of the problem the modern protocol still solves: partition ownership must be recomputed and redistributed whenever group membership changes, and every generation of the protocol is an answer to how to do that recomputation with minimal disruption. Coverage of the ZooKeeper-to-KRaft transition itself is out of scope for this harvest; this row only establishes the historical shape of the rebalance problem.

members.subject: Group coordinator, generation ID, and the JoinGroup/SyncGroup/Heartbeat/LeaveGroup RPCs (classic protocol)
members.description: The Kafka protocol guide states 'each group in the cluster is assigned to one of the brokers (its group coordinator) to facilitate group management.' On a rebalance, 'when new members join an existing group, all previous members are required to rejoin by sending a new join group request'; the coordinator then 'select[s] one member to be the group leader and a protocol which is supported by all members.' Critically, assignment computation itself happens on the client, not the broker, in this classic protocol: 'the sync group request is used by the group leader to assign state (e.g. partition assignments) to all members of the current generation... only the leader provides the group's assignment.' The coordinator increments a generation ID on every rebalance and rejects stale-generation requests, forcing lagging members to rejoin. Heartbeat requests keep a member's session alive; if none arrive within session.timeout.ms 'the member will be kicked out of the group.' LeaveGroup exists because it 'is preferred over letting the session timeout expire since it allows the group to rebalance faster' -- an explicit exit is detected immediately, whereas silence is only detected after the full timeout window.

members.subject: Rebalance triggers
members.description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc lists the conditions that cause the group coordinator to trigger a rebalance: a new consumer joining the group, an existing consumer leaving (gracefully or by crash/timeout), and topic metadata changes such as new partitions being added to a subscribed topic. Each of these events changes group membership or the set of resources to divide, so the coordinator must recompute and redistribute partition ownership across the current members.

members.subject: Rebalances are stop-the-world for the whole group, not just the changed member
members.description: Under the classic eager rebalance protocol, when group membership changes -- a new consumer joins, one leaves, one is evicted for missing max.poll.interval.ms, or partition count changes -- ALL consumers in the group temporarily pause processing, commit their current offsets, and revoke ownership of every partition they held, before partitions are reassigned. This is not scoped to the consumer that changed: even a member consuming an entirely unrelated set of partitions pauses. In environments with frequent restarts (rolling deploys, transient network blips, autoscaling), this compounds into 'rebalance storms' where overlapping restarts chain into repeated full-group pauses, and one case study found a rolling restart of 5 consumers triggering 10 separate rebalances. The documented mitigations are static group membership (group.instance.id) so brief restarts don't drop a member from the group at all, and the CooperativeStickyAssignor (default assignor pairing since Kafka 2.4+/3.0), which reassigns only the specific partitions that must move instead of revoking everything.

principle: A partition-level stall is invisible on every signal except per-partition lag, and in this row set lag itself is only defined inside a hands-on lab rather than as a documented concept
because: A bad deserializer or a slow handler doesn't crash the consumer or show up group-wide -- it just stops one partition's CURRENT-OFFSET from closing the gap to LOG-END-OFFSET while every other partition reads clean -- but the row that actually defines CURRENT-OFFSET and LOG-END-OFFSET only exists because an exercise walked someone through reading them off a CLI, meaning a reader who never runs the lab has no vocabulary for the exact symptom the poison-pill and livelock rows describe.

members.subject: Poison pill messages block the whole partition
members.description: When a consumer's deserializer cannot parse a record (commonly because a producer changed serialization format, or the consumer is configured with the wrong key/value deserializer), the default behavior is that the exception is thrown before the offset for that record is ever advanced. Because the consumer re-polls and hits the same record again, it enters an infinite retry loop against that one 'poison pill' message, and every other message queued behind it on that partition is starved indefinitely -- this is not a whole-consumer crash, it is a silent partition-level stall that can go unnoticed until lag alarms fire. Confluent's own guidance is to never let deserialization exceptions propagate up to block re-polling; the documented fix (for the Java/Spring stack) is a wrapping ErrorHandlingDeserializer that catches the failure, returns null plus a DeserializationException header, and routes the record to a dead-letter topic via a recoverer, which lets the offset advance past the bad record.

members.subject: Re-derive why a poison pill stalls one partition and not the topic
members.description: Reason from the single-integer-offset model rather than from a remembered answer. Then list the exits (skip, dead-letter topic, retry with backoff) and name the guarantee each one costs you.

members.subject: Consumer lag: CURRENT-OFFSET versus LOG-END-OFFSET
members.description: Confluent's Kafka Technical Fundamentals lab defines lag as 'how many messages have been written to the current partition but have not yet been consumed', and walks through reading it from the consumer-group listing where 'the LOG-END-OFFSET shows the offset to which the next message would be written' against the group's CURRENT-OFFSET. Lag is the operational counterpart to everything the offset rows describe: a group that is committing correctly but processing too slowly looks healthy by every other signal and is only visible as growing lag, and because lag is per partition, a single hot or stalled partition (see the poison-pill trap, K-020) shows as one partition's lag climbing while the group's other partitions read zero. It is also the measurement that makes the max.poll.interval.ms tradeoff (K-036, K-038) concrete rather than theoretical. Added by audit: lag appears in this run only inside exercise K-026, so a reader who does not run the lab never encounters it -- an operational must-know reachable only by doing.

members.subject: Confluent Kafka Technical Fundamentals -- Fun Exercise Book (browser-based Gitpod lab)
members.description: Two linked hands-on activities. Activity 1 walks through signing up for Confluent Cloud, installing its CLI, and using it to create a topic and produce/consume. Activity 2 is a browser-based Gitpod lab (no local install required) that has the reader inspect consumer-group describe output, specifically the CURRENT-OFFSET and LOG-END-OFFSET columns, to see that the next-read position equals the next-write position when caught up; produce a message with a specific key and observe which partition it lands on to demonstrate key-based routing; and read the LAG column to understand how many produced-but-unconsumed messages sit on a partition. It also has the reader stop/restart consumers and observe consumer-group behavior, though it does not walk through rebalancing mechanics explicitly. Confirmed live and working when fetched, both activities have concrete steps and cleanup instructions.

principle: A Schema Registry compatibility mode is not a validation setting, it is a pre-committed answer to which side — producer or consumer — upgrades first
because: The mode's name, its default, its per-subject override, its transitive variant, and its escape hatch (NONE) all function as one thing: a binding rollout-order commitment, which is why the direction gets inverted so often (A-025) and why a downstream technology like Kafka Streams can still fail even when the mode is technically satisfied (A-014).

members.subject: Backward compatibility vs. forward compatibility (definitions)
members.description: This pairing is foundational orientation for the whole schema-evolution space: backward compatibility lets you upgrade consumers before producers (and rewind a consumer to the start of a topic and still read old data with the new schema); forward compatibility lets you upgrade producers before consumers. Without this distinction a reader cannot correctly reason about upgrade ordering at all, which is why it sits at orientation rather than operation.

members.subject: Schema Registry compatibility modes: BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL
members.description: BACKWARD is the Schema Registry default and Confluent's stated preferred mode for Kafka specifically because it lets you rewind consumers to the beginning of a topic and still deserialize with the new schema. FULL is the most restrictive but lets producers and consumers upgrade independently in any order, which matters when you cannot guarantee upgrade sequencing across teams. Getting the allowed-changes list wrong (e.g. adding a required field under BACKWARD) fails the registry's compatibility check immediately at schema-registration time - a visible, operation-level failure.

members.subject: Schema Registry's default compatibility mode is BACKWARD
members.description: Confluent's schema-evolution documentation states that 'the default compatibility mode is BACKWARD', checked non-transitively against the latest registered version only. This matters more than a default usually does, because BACKWARD is not a neutral setting: per the same page it permits adding optional fields and removing fields, and it fixes the rollout order -- consumers upgrade before producers. A team that never touches the compatibility configuration has therefore made a governance decision (A-033) without knowing it, and will find out at the first rollout where a producer ships first. It also explains a common surprise: a schema change rejected by a registry nobody configured is being rejected by BACKWARD's rules specifically, not by generic 'schema validation'. Added by audit: six rows in this set discuss selecting among the modes (A-001, A-022, A-025, A-033, A-043, A-045) and none states which one applies by default.

members.subject: BACKWARD compatibility direction
members.description: BACKWARD compatibility means a schema registered as BACKWARD-compatible allows consumers using the NEW schema to read data produced with the LAST (older) schema. The common mistake is assuming BACKWARD means 'old consumers can still read new data' (that is actually FORWARD compatibility). Because of this, the safe rollout order under BACKWARD compatibility is: upgrade all consumers first, then let producers start writing the new schema. Teams that roll out in the opposite order (producers first) under a BACKWARD-only contract can have old consumers choke on data they cannot deserialize, or new consumers running ahead of a producer upgrade misinterpret events. Confluent's own docs are explicit that FORWARD compatibility, by contrast, requires producers to upgrade first.

members.subject: Compatibility mode choice dictates rollout order
members.description: Confluent's schema evolution documentation (opened directly) ties each compatibility mode to a specific safe deployment order: BACKWARD requires all consumers to upgrade before producers start writing the new schema; FORWARD requires all producers to upgrade first, and old data must be fully drained/unavailable before consumers upgrade; FULL allows producers and consumers to upgrade independently in any order, at the cost of requiring every change to satisfy both directions simultaneously (e.g., new fields must carry defaults so both old and new schemas can decode each other's data). TRANSITIVE variants extend the same guarantee across every historical schema version, not just the immediately previous one — meaningfully different in a topic with many schema versions in flight, since non-transitive BACKWARD only checks against the last version and can silently accumulate incompatibilities two or three versions back. Picking a mode is therefore a decision about which team (producer or consumer owners) is forced to move first during every future change, and that constraint is easy to discover only once a rollout goes wrong.

members.subject: Kafka Streams requires BACKWARD-only compatibility and upgrade-before-producer ordering
members.description: This is a specific operational constraint that breaks visibly and immediately if violated: if a producer starts writing a new (even backward-compatible) schema version before the downstream Streams app has been upgraded, the Streams app fails to process the new records correctly. It's called out separately from the general BACKWARD/FORWARD/FULL mode description because it's a constraint on a specific consumer technology (Kafka Streams), not a property of the compatibility mode itself. [MERGED FROM A-040] The underlying reason: a Streams application reads both new input topics and its own older internal state stores, so it must tolerate old data under a new schema.

members.subject: Per-subject vs. global compatibility configuration in Schema Registry
members.description: Knowing this override relationship is necessary to use the registry correctly day-to-day: an operator who only checks the global config can be surprised by a subject that was deliberately configured looser or stricter. This is a mechanical configuration fact, not a strategy choice, so it sits at operation.

members.subject: NONE compatibility mode disables schema safety checks
members.description: This is a judgment-level trap-adjacent concept: choosing NONE removes the registry's only automated safety net, and the consequence (a deserialization failure in production) surfaces later, at read time on whichever consumer first encounters the incompatible data, not at schema-registration time. It's sometimes a legitimate choice (e.g. during early prototyping, or for topics with a single tightly-coupled producer/consumer pair deployed atomically) but the decision to use it needs to be deliberate, not a default left unconfigured.

members.subject: Transitive compatibility checking (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE / FORWARD_TRANSITIVE / FULL_TRANSITIVE) vs. latest-only
members.description: Choosing transitive vs. non-transitive is a judgment call whose cost is invisible until a consumer that's several versions behind - not just one version behind - tries to read current data, or a producer several versions behind writes into a topic a fresh consumer must read. Non-transitive checking is cheaper and looser day-to-day but silently permits a chain of individually-compatible changes that are not jointly compatible across the full history; transitive checking catches that at registration time but is stricter and can block legitimate-looking single-step changes. Confluent's docs present this explicitly as a config choice (global default or per-subject).

members.subject: Derive rollout order from a compatibility mode, and back again
members.description: Start from the mode and derive the order. Then reverse: given a deployment where you cannot upgrade all consumers first, derive which mode you are forced into. Reversing is the half that catches a memorized mapping, because the direction of BACKWARD is the single most commonly inverted fact in this area.

principle: The entire offset model follows from Kafka keeping the broker stateless and pushing all consumption bookkeeping onto the client
because: The original design pushed all per-consumer state off the broker and onto the client, which is what let Kafka collapse a consumer's progress into one integer; that same collapse is what forces the API to distinguish the read position from the committed position and to insist you commit the next offset rather than the last one, since a single number can't represent 'processed' and 'safe to resume from' separately unless the convention pins down exactly which one it means.

members.subject: Original design: stateless broker, consumer-held position, retention-driven deletion
members.description: The original Kafka design presentation by its creators (Kreps, Narkhede, Rao at LinkedIn), archived as an official attachment on the Apache Kafka project wiki, states the principle as 'Efficiency #3: Stateless Broker' -- 'each consumer maintains its own state' and 'message deletion driven by retention policy, not by tracking consumption,' which the authors call 'acceptable in practice' and note enables a 'rewindable consumer.' This is a foundational architectural decision that explains why Kafka retains messages for a fixed window regardless of consumption (unlike a traditional queue that deletes on ack): the broker's job is to be a dumb, efficient append-only log, and all consumption bookkeeping is pushed to the client side. It directly explains why consumer position being 'just a single integer' (separate row) is possible at all -- the broker has no competing notion of per-message state to reconcile it against.

members.subject: Consumer position as a single integer offset
members.description: The Kafka design documentation states: 'the position of a consumer in each partition is just a single integer, the offset of the next message to consume.' This is a deliberate departure from traditional message queues (e.g. JMS brokers), which must track per-message acknowledgment state for every consumer. Because position is one number per partition, it is cheap to store, cheap to advance, and cheap to rewind: a consumer can deliberately seek backward to an earlier offset to reprocess data, which most point-to-point queueing systems do not support.

members.subject: Position vs committed position, and the n+1 commit rule
members.description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc is explicit that 'there are actually two notions of position relevant to the user of the consumer: The position of the consumer gives the offset of the next record that will be given out. It will be one larger than the highest offset the consumer has seen in that partition... The committed position is the last offset that has been stored securely. Should the process fail and restart, this is the offset that the consumer will recover to.' It then states the rule that manual-commit code gets wrong: 'Note: The committed offset should always be the offset of the next message that your application will read. Thus, when calling commitSync(offsets) you should use nextRecordToBeProcessed.offset() or if ConsumerRecords is exhausted already ConsumerRecords.nextOffsets() instead.' Committing record.offset() rather than record.offset()+1 does not fail loudly -- it silently reprocesses exactly one record per commit, forever, which is invisible in any test that tolerates at-least-once. The same section adds a second correction to the naive mental model: 'offsets are not guaranteed to be consecutive (such as compacted topic or when records have been produced using transactions)', so code that infers message loss from a gap in offsets is wrong. Added by audit: K-002 establishes that position is a single integer at orientation depth and K-006 covers commitSync vs commitAsync, but no row in the set states what value to commit.

principle: Two separate fixes attack the same synchronous-barrier problem from opposite ends: shrink what a rebalance revokes, or remove the client-side computation step entirely
because: KIP-429 keeps the barrier but adds an owned-partitions field so only genuinely-moving partitions get revoked across a second, smaller round; KIP-848 removes the barrier altogether by making assignment a server-computed, independently-reconciled target state; group.protocol is the literal switch between an old-era client that fully participates in the barrier and a new-era client that does not.

members.subject: Cooperative/incremental rebalancing replaces stop-the-world eager rebalancing
members.description: The original eager protocol forces every consumer to revoke all of its partitions at the start of every rebalance, even the ones it will be reassigned right back afterward, causing avoidable processing downtime. KIP-429's cooperative approach lets consumers retain currently-owned partitions through the rebalance's join phase; a partition is only revoked, via a follow-up rebalance, if its ownership is genuinely changing. This 'minimizes partition movement' when paired with a sticky assignor. The KIP names the CooperativeStickyAssignor as the built-in implementation and adds an onPartitionsLost() callback distinguishing voluntary revocation from forced ejection from the group. The KIP is explicit about the tradeoff: cooperative rebalancing 'is really expecting the plug-in assignor to be sticky' -- with a non-sticky assignor it merely adds extra rebalance rounds without reducing cost, and the upgrade path itself requires two rolling bounces of the fleet instead of one.

members.subject: Cooperative rebalancing internals: owned-partitions field and consecutive-rebalance-as-barrier
members.description: Mechanistically, KIP-429 changes what information flows through the group protocol: subscriptions now carry an 'owned partitions' field so the assignor knows what each member currently holds, not just what it wants. Rather than a single global synchronization point where every member must revoke before anyone gets a new assignment, the protocol uses consecutive rebalances as the synchronization mechanism -- a member holding a partition that is moving keeps it through the first rebalance round, then revokes it (triggering a second, smaller rebalance) once the target owner is known. Listener callbacks only fire for partitions that actually changed, not for the full assignment on every rebalance, which is a behavioral change from the eager protocol's listener semantics.

members.subject: Next-generation consumer group protocol moves assignment computation server-side
members.description: KIP-848's stated motivation is operational: 'we have had many bugs in the rebalance protocol over the last years and the majority of them required client side bug fixes,' and in managed/cloud environments fixing a protocol bug 'depend[s] on the adoption of the clients.' The classic protocol's global synchronization barrier means 'a single misbehaving consumer can take down or disturb the whole group because a rebalance of the whole group is required whenever a consumer joins, leaves or fails.' The new protocol makes assignment declarative and server-driven: 'the assignor defines the desired state for the group and let the group coordinator converge to it,' so members reconcile toward their target assignment independently and a partial group update (one member's assignment changing) no longer requires a full-group rebalance. Enabling it requires setting group.protocol=consumer on the client; once active, several classic-protocol consumer configs (heartbeat.interval.ms, session.timeout.ms, partition.assignment.strategy) are no longer used -- their broker-side equivalents (group.consumer.*) apply instead. Stated tradeoffs: client-side custom assignors are not supported under the new protocol, and Kafka Connect does not support it as of the source reviewed. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Summary asserts '(default from Kafka 4.0, group.protocol=consumer)'. KIP-848 itself states: 'In the beginning, the new protocol will be disabled by default. We envision enabling it by default in a future major release of Kafka.' The Kafka 4.3 consumer-configs page gives group.protocol Default: classic. The parenthetical is contradicted by its own cited source, by row K-010, and by this row's own description ('Enabling it requires setting group.protocol=consumer on the client').]

members.subject: group.protocol config selects classic vs next-generation rebalancing
members.description: group.protocol is documented as 'the group protocol that the consumer uses,' defaulting to classic. Setting it to consumer opts the client into the KIP-848 protocol. Per the consumer-rebalance-protocol operations page, migration supports both offline and online (rolling) upgrade paths, and once a consumer runs the new protocol, legacy configs like heartbeat.interval.ms, session.timeout.ms, and partition.assignment.strategy become unavailable on that client -- the equivalent broker-side group.consumer.* settings govern those values instead. Known limitations at time of writing: client-side custom assignors are unsupported, and rack-aware assignment strategies are not yet fully supported under the new protocol.

principle: Where the version identifier lives — URL path, query string, or content-negotiation header — decides what a future change gets coupled to
because: Path versioning couples the version to the URL itself and to gateway routing, so migrating consumers means changing every call site and every co-located service must agree on one mechanism; query-string versioning is only safe once path stability is already guaranteed; header/media-type versioning decouples the version from the URL at the cost of a pastable link — three schemes solving the same problem by choosing a different thing to couple the version to, which is why no scheme is actually free.

members.subject: Protobuf's tiered classification of changes: wire-safe, wire-unsafe, and conditionally-safe
members.description: This three-way classification is itself a judgment tool: the middle band ('wire-compatible' but requiring careful rollout) is where teams get burned, because the change type-checks and appears safe in isolation, but produces different results depending on which side (producer or consumer) upgrades first - the cost of getting the rollout order wrong surfaces at scale, not in a single local test. Choosing to make one of these conditionally-safe changes without a deliberate rollout plan is exactly the kind of correct-syntax-wrong-decision failure that defines judgment-level knowledge. [AUDIT depth judgment->operation: Protobuf's wire-safe / wire-unsafe / conditionally-safe classification is the lookup table you need to make a schema change correctly in the normal case; without it the change breaks immediately and visibly at decode. Its siblings A-020, A-021 and A-026 are all operation. (Arguable: the conditionally-safe band carries rollout-ordering judgment; better to split that out than to tier the whole row up.)]

members.subject: No-versioning / continuous compatible-evolution strategy (Stripe's rolling dates)
members.description: Per Stripe's own versioning writeup, a new account is automatically pinned to the latest version on its first API call; it keeps working on that version indefinitely unless the developer explicitly upgrades (via the dashboard) or overrides per-request with a Stripe-Version header. Each dated version bundles a small set of changes rather than a large breaking rewrite, so upgrades are incremental rather than all-or-nothing. Choosing this strategy versus versioned major releases is a governance decision: it demands building and maintaining a per-version compatibility-transform layer (see the companion mechanism row on Stripe's transformer architecture) in exchange for consumers never facing a hard cutover deadline.

members.subject: Schema Registry's default compatibility mode is BACKWARD
members.description: Confluent's schema-evolution documentation states that 'the default compatibility mode is BACKWARD', checked non-transitively against the latest registered version only. This matters more than a default usually does, because BACKWARD is not a neutral setting: per the same page it permits adding optional fields and removing fields, and it fixes the rollout order -- consumers upgrade before producers. A team that never touches the compatibility configuration has therefore made a governance decision (A-033) without knowing it, and will find out at the first rollout where a producer ships first. It also explains a common surprise: a schema change rejected by a registry nobody configured is being rejected by BACKWARD's rules specifically, not by generic 'schema validation'. Added by audit: six rows in this set discuss selecting among the modes (A-001, A-022, A-025, A-033, A-043, A-045) and none states which one applies by default.

members.subject: Google AIP: recommended 180-day deprecation window for beta releases
members.description: This is a concrete instance of the deprecation-window-length decision: too short and consumers who haven't migrated get broken; too long and the provider carries maintenance cost for versions it wants to retire. AIP-185 ties the number to release maturity (beta gets a shorter guaranteed window than GA), which is itself a judgment about how much stability a given maturity label should promise.

members.subject: Deprecation header as a complete deprecation process
members.description: RFC 8594 (the Sunset HTTP header) is explicit about its own limits: it defines the header as a way to 'signal intent so that applications using resources may get a warning ahead of time,' and states plainly that 'what an appropriate reaction is... is outside the scope of this specification.' The RFC also says the Sunset header is not even appropriate for the early stage where an API is deprecated-but-still-working — only for the final unresponsive stage — meaning header-only signaling misses the whole early phase of a real deprecation. Zalando's public API guidelines, opened directly, mandate a much larger process around the header: the deprecation must be reflected in the machine-readable API spec (`deprecated: true` with a migration description), the provider must get explicit consumer consent to a sunset date before shutting anything down, and the provider must monitor actual usage of the deprecated surface in production to know when it's safe to sunset — none of which a response header alone provides.

members.subject: Azure Breaking Change Review Board approval gate
members.description: This documents breaking-change governance as an organizational process, not just a technical rule: a human review board sits in the approval path specifically because the cost of an unreviewed breaking change surfaces late, at the customer's next deployment, not at merge time. Azure additionally requires an azure-deprecating response header communicating what is retiring, the retirement date, and a documentation URL - the same header-plus-link pattern as RFC 9745/8594, applied as a mandatory internal policy rather than an optional client courtesy. [AUDIT viable->wounded: 'pull requests failing the policy check cannot merge without that approval' is not in the cited Azure Guidelines.md -- the document contains no pull-request or merge-gating text. The review-board rule itself is quoted correctly ('DO NOT introduce any breaking changes into the service'; breaking changes 'allowable... if approved by the Azure Breaking Change Reviewers but only following ample communication to customers and a lengthy deprecation period'). Drop the unsupported merge-gate clause.]

members.subject: Ordering constraint between Deprecation and Sunset header dates
members.description: This is a specific correctness rule for using the two headers together: violating it produces a logically incoherent signal to clients (retirement before notice of deprecation), which breaks the trust a client places in the headers to plan its migration. It sits at the operation level because getting it wrong is a visible, mechanical spec violation, not a strategic tradeoff.

members.subject: Date-based API versioning as a governance model
members.description: Stripe's own engineering blog (opened directly) explains why they rejected major-version-number versioning: 'changes between versions being so big and so impactful for users that it's almost as painful as re-integrating from scratch,' and that scheme also forces a binary choice of freezing consumers on an old major version or cutting them off. Instead, Stripe pins every account to the API version active when it was created (a date, e.g. 2024-04-10); every incoming request for an older-pinned account is passed through a chain of small, per-change version-shim modules so that the internal service logic only ever has to implement the current schema, not a matrix of if/else branches for every historical version. This is a genuine judgment-level tradeoff: it adds real internal maintenance cost (an ever-growing chain of shims) in exchange for never forcing a disruptive re-integration on consumers, and is presented as a deliberate alternative to both URI-path and header-based major versioning.

principle: Manual commit APIs and the rebalance-revoke callback exist to answer the same question from two directions: how do you commit work Kafka doesn't know is unfinished, before Kafka takes the partition away
because: The client's lack of thread-safety is what forces decoupled processing to route commits back through the single-threaded consumer rather than committing from a worker thread directly; the sync/async split then trades that discipline for throughput in steady state; and the revoke callback is the one moment manual code gets a guaranteed last chance to commit before ownership actually moves, which is exactly why practitioners reach for the blocking call there and nowhere else in the loop.

members.subject: KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe
members.description: The javadoc states plainly: 'The Kafka consumer is NOT thread-safe. It is the responsibility of the user to ensure that multi-threaded access is properly synchronized. Un-synchronized access will result in ConcurrentModificationException.' The single documented exception is wakeup(), which 'can safely be used from an external thread to interrupt an active operation,' causing the blocked call to throw WakeupException so the consumer can shut down cleanly. This constraint is why the decoupled-processing pattern (separate row) requires care: the worker threads must never call consumer methods directly.

members.subject: Decoupling consumption from processing via a worker thread pool
members.description: The javadoc's recommended pattern for handling slow or variable-latency processing: 'move message processing to another thread, which allows the consumer to continue calling poll while the processor is still working,' combined with disabling automatic commits and manually committing 'processed offsets for records only after the thread has finished handling them.' This is presented as a choice among two documented multi-threading patterns -- one-consumer-per-thread (simplest, 'often the fastest', but uses more TCP connections) versus decoupled consumption/processing (a single consumer feeding a thread pool via a blocking queue, which 'allows independently scaling the number of consumers and processors' but requires careful coordination so offsets are only committed for fully-processed records).

members.subject: commitSync vs commitAsync
members.description: When manual commit is chosen, KafkaConsumer exposes commitSync(), which blocks the calling thread until the commit either succeeds or fails, and commitAsync(), which returns immediately and optionally invokes a callback. The javadoc frames manual control as necessary whenever 'the consumption of the messages is coupled with some processing logic and hence a message should not be considered as consumed until it is completed processing' -- i.e. whenever correctness requires the commit to happen only after work is done, not on a timer. It also states the convention that 'the committed offset should always be the offset of the next message that your application will read,' not the offset of the last message read.

members.subject: Choosing commitSync vs commitAsync is a throughput/safety tradeoff, not a correctness switch
members.description: commitSync() blocks the polling thread until the broker acknowledges the commit, and it will automatically retry on retriable errors -- this is reliable but forces the consumer loop to pay a network round-trip and reduces throughput. commitAsync() does not block and optionally takes a callback for success/failure, which is faster under load, but a failed async commit is not automatically retried by the client, and because commits can be reordered, blindly retrying a stale async commit risk overwriting a later, valid commit with an older offset. The judgment call practitioners have to make deliberately: use commitAsync() in the steady-state poll loop for throughput, but call commitSync() on rebalance (in the revoke callback) and on shutdown, where a blocking guarantee actually matters and there's no 'next commit' to fall back on.

members.subject: ConsumerRebalanceListener callbacks
members.description: The javadoc describes ConsumerRebalanceListener as the hook for application-level logic around rebalances. onPartitionsRevoked(Collection) is called when partitions are about to be taken from the consumer, giving the application a chance to 'finish necessary application-level logic such as state cleanup, manual offset commits' before losing ownership. onPartitionsAssigned(Collection) is called after new partitions are assigned, letting the consumer call seek() to initialize its read position for those partitions if it needs something other than the last committed offset. Without registering this listener, applications cannot reliably commit in-flight work before a partition moves to another consumer.

members.subject: Confluent Apache Kafka for Python Developers -- Hands On: Use the Python Consumer Class
members.description: This is a distinct, more advanced exercise from the 'Apache Kafka for Python Developers' course (separate from the Kafka 101 consumer exercise). The reader builds consumer.py with group.id='hello_group', auto.offset.reset='earliest', and enable.auto.commit=False, implements an assignment_callback() to observe partition assignment, polls with consumer.poll(1.0), and manually commits offsets with consumer.commit(event) after processing. The exercise then has the reader add and remove consumer instances from the group to observe live rebalancing behavior. Confirmed live and working when fetched, with concrete code and steps.

principle: auto.offset.reset is not a one-time startup choice; it re-fires later, invisibly, whenever a committed offset stops being usable
because: The setting only activates when there is no usable committed offset, but that condition doesn't just occur at first launch -- offsets.retention.minutes can expire an old commit for a low-traffic group, or a group can be mistaken for new -- so the same two-value choice made once, deliberately, at setup time can later trigger unannounced, on its own schedule, as either a mass replay or a silent multi-message loss, and the operator who set it may never be the one present when it fires.

members.subject: auto.offset.reset governs behavior when no valid committed offset exists
members.description: Documented as controlling 'what to do when there is no initial offset in Kafka or if the current offset does not exist any more on the server,' with a default of latest. A brand-new consumer group, or a group whose committed offset has aged out of the topic's retention window, hits this fallback. 'latest' starts consumption from the newest record, silently skipping any backlog -- appropriate for consumers that only care about new events. 'earliest' starts from the oldest retained record, reprocessing the full available history -- appropriate when completeness matters more than avoiding reprocessing. This setting only applies in the absence of a usable committed offset; it does not override an existing valid commit. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Cited page https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/consumer-configs/ documents FOUR values for auto.offset.reset (earliest, latest, by_duration:<duration>, none); the row presents only two. 'none' (throw if no committed offset) is the fail-loud option and the direct remedy for the K-041 trap. Incomplete against its own source at operation depth. Default 'latest' is confirmed correct.]

members.subject: auto.offset.reset triggers surprise replay or silent data skip
members.description: auto.offset.reset controls what a consumer does when it has no committed offset for a partition or the committed offset is out of range -- but people configure it once at setup and forget it can activate later, unexpectedly, e.g. when offsets.retention.minutes expires an old committed offset for a low-traffic consumer group, or a consumer group is inadvertently treated as new. The two settings then fail in opposite, equally dangerous directions: 'earliest' can replay millions of historical messages the consumer never intended to reprocess, while 'latest' silently skips everything already in the log, permanently losing any messages produced between the last real commit and the reset event. Neither is a 'safe default' -- the choice has to be a deliberate decision tied to how the consumer's downstream side effects behave under replay versus loss.

principle: The Deprecation and Sunset headers are a notification layer, and every real deprecation decision happens outside them
because: The headers themselves only carry a date and a link; RFC 8594 says outright that what to do about that date is out of scope, which is exactly the gap that Zalando's consent-and-monitoring process, Azure's review board, and the window-length numbers from Google (180 days) and Microsoft Graph (24-36 months) all fill in — the header signals, but consent, review, and window length are where the actual governance judgment lives.

members.subject: Sunset HTTP response header (RFC 8594)
members.description: The RFC frames the sunset date as a hint, not a guarantee - clients should not treat it as a hard contractual deadline, only as a signal to plan migration. It is distinct from HTTP caching headers: Sunset communicates resource retirement, not content freshness. Documented use cases include temporary resources, service migrations, regulatory retention windows, and API deprecation specifically.

members.subject: Deprecation HTTP response header (RFC 9745)
members.description: The RFC pairs the header with a 'deprecation' link relation that servers can use to point clients at documentation about the deprecation policy or migration path. It explicitly integrates with the Sunset header from RFC 8594: per RFC 9745, the timestamp in Sunset must not precede the Deprecation date, since deprecation (advance notice) logically precedes sunset (actual retirement).

members.subject: Ordering constraint between Deprecation and Sunset header dates
members.description: This is a specific correctness rule for using the two headers together: violating it produces a logically incoherent signal to clients (retirement before notice of deprecation), which breaks the trust a client places in the headers to plan its migration. It sits at the operation level because getting it wrong is a visible, mechanical spec violation, not a strategic tradeoff.

members.subject: Deprecation and Sunset link relations for policy documentation
members.description: The header alone only carries a date; the link relation is how a provider attaches an explanation. Zalando's own deprecation guidance builds on the same pattern, requiring producers to add a description explaining the deprecation and provide a migration manual - the RFC-level link relation is the standard mechanism for surfacing exactly that kind of documentation to automated clients rather than only humans reading changelogs.

members.subject: Deprecation header as a complete deprecation process
members.description: RFC 8594 (the Sunset HTTP header) is explicit about its own limits: it defines the header as a way to 'signal intent so that applications using resources may get a warning ahead of time,' and states plainly that 'what an appropriate reaction is... is outside the scope of this specification.' The RFC also says the Sunset header is not even appropriate for the early stage where an API is deprecated-but-still-working — only for the final unresponsive stage — meaning header-only signaling misses the whole early phase of a real deprecation. Zalando's public API guidelines, opened directly, mandate a much larger process around the header: the deprecation must be reflected in the machine-readable API spec (`deprecated: true` with a migration description), the provider must get explicit consumer consent to a sunset date before shutting anything down, and the provider must monitor actual usage of the deprecated surface in production to know when it's safe to sunset — none of which a response header alone provides.

members.subject: Deprecation and sunset process requirements
members.description: Zalando's public REST API guidelines (opened directly) lay out the concrete governance steps beyond headers: (1) the deprecation must be part of the API specification itself, with `deprecated: true` and a migration description, so it's discoverable by tooling, not just by inspecting live traffic; (2) for a sunset (full shutdown) to be permitted, the API owner must obtain explicit consumer/partner consent to a specific sunset date, negotiated as part of granting access in the first place for external partners; (3) the provider must monitor production usage of the deprecated surface to know whether consumers have actually migrated, and clients are expected to monitor the Deprecation/Sunset headers themselves and alert on them. This is a judgment call, not a mechanical step, because the 'reasonable time span' for the deprecation window has to be negotiated per-consumer and isn't dictated by the spec.

members.subject: Zalando deprecation process: deprecated:true plus consumer consent before sunset
members.description: This is a governance-process rule, not just a syntax rule: the mechanical marking (deprecated: true) is easy to get right, but the consent-gathering step is a judgment-laden negotiation whose cost surfaces late - at cutover, if any consumer never gave consent or never migrated, the shutdown either breaks that consumer or has to slip. Zalando additionally requires the Deprecation and Sunset headers to reflect the earliest timestamp when multiple elements are deprecated at once, and requires clients to build monitoring/alerting on those headers rather than relying on best-effort awareness.

members.subject: Azure Breaking Change Review Board approval gate
members.description: This documents breaking-change governance as an organizational process, not just a technical rule: a human review board sits in the approval path specifically because the cost of an unreviewed breaking change surfaces late, at the customer's next deployment, not at merge time. Azure additionally requires an azure-deprecating response header communicating what is retiring, the retirement date, and a documentation URL - the same header-plus-link pattern as RFC 9745/8594, applied as a mandatory internal policy rather than an optional client courtesy. members.subject: Google AIP: recommended 180-day deprecation window for beta releases
members.description: This is a concrete instance of the deprecation-window-length decision: too short and consumers who haven't migrated get broken; too long and the provider carries maintenance cost for versions it wants to retire. AIP-185 ties the number to release maturity (beta gets a shorter guaranteed window than GA), which is itself a judgment about how much stability a given maturity label should promise.

members.subject: Microsoft Graph deprecation window: 24-36 months notice
members.description: This is a concrete, named organizational answer to 'how long should a deprecation window be' - a judgment-level decision the AIP-185 180-day beta figure sits in contrast to. The gap (180 days for a Google beta vs. 24-36 months for Microsoft Graph GA) reflects that maturity label (beta vs. GA) is itself the variable governing how long a provider is willing to commit to. Choosing a window that's too short for the surface's maturity is a decision whose cost only appears when consumers who relied on the longer implicit guarantee get broken. principle: Consumer-driven contract testing is deliberately narrow, and its value depends on not asking it to be an integration test
because: Pact's own 'test button, not house fire' framing only verifies the specific interaction shape a consumer actually exercises, which is exactly why authorship matters — consumer-driven contracts define what counts as breaking — and exactly why treating passing contract tests as integration coverage is a documented failure mode rather than a hypothetical one; the two workshops drill the identical narrow-scope discipline in different stacks, and the closing drill forces naming the failure class neither test catches.

members.subject: Pact: consumer-driven contract testing workflow
members.description: This is orientation-level because it establishes what consumer-driven contract testing fundamentally is and how it differs from schema-first approaches: rather than a static schema describing every possible interaction, the contract is generated from the consumer's actual usage, so 'only parts of the communication that are actually used by the consumer(s) get tested.' Pact's own docs describe the analogy of testing a smoke alarm's contract with its test button rather than by setting the house on fire - i.e. verifying integration without running both real services together end-to-end.

members.subject: Consumer-driven contract ownership
members.description: Martin Fowler's original Consumer-Driven Contracts article (opened directly) describes the pattern as consumer contracts expressing consumer expectations, adopted by the provider so that 'consumer contracts effectively define which parts of that provider contract currently support the business value realized by the system.' This is a judgment-level design decision, not a mechanical testing choice: it determines who has authority over what counts as a breaking change. A provider-authored contract can change anything the provider didn't anticipate a consumer needing; a consumer-driven contract makes any change that breaks a registered consumer expectation visible before release, at the cost of providers now depending on consumers actually maintaining and publishing their contracts (typically via a broker).

members.subject: Contract tests as a substitute for integration tests
members.description: Microsoft's public Engineering Fundamentals Playbook, in its consumer-driven contract (CDC) testing chapter (opened directly), states: 'Contract tests are not the place to verify internal business logic and correctness of the consumer,' and cautions that CDC scope must be kept tight so it doesn't blur into 'other higher level functional testing layers.' The practical failure mode this guards against: a team adopts Pact-style contract tests, sees them pass, and treats that as equivalent coverage to a full integration or end-to-end suite — but contract tests only verify that a specific consumer-provider interaction matches an agreed shape; they say nothing about network behavior, infra, multi-service call sequencing, or a consumer's own business logic. Related literature (Martin Fowler's original Consumer-Driven Contracts article, opened directly) frames CDC instead as a design discipline: consumers author the contract to make the provider's evolution safe for them, which is a narrower and different goal than end-to-end verification.

members.subject: Pact JS contract testing workshop
members.description: Confirmed by opening both the docs.pact.io landing page and the linked GitHub repo directly. Real, actively maintained repository (159 stars, 171 forks, 239 commits, open PRs/issues as of this check) under the official pact-foundation GitHub org. The README states the workshop takes 1-2 hours depending on depth. It progresses through 13 git-branch-tagged steps: writing a consumer test against a mock provider, generating a Pact contract, verifying it against a real Express provider, handling provider states, adding authorization, and finally publishing/consuming contracts via a Pact Broker (steps 11-12 need a locally-Dockerized broker or a PactFlow account). This is squarely in scope: consumer-driven contract testing hands-on practice.

members.description: Confirmed by opening the GitHub repo directly: pact-foundation/pact-workshop-jvm-spring, 118 stars, 81 forks, 57 commits, Docker Compose support, current Spring Boot patterns, no signs of abandonment. The README states the workshop takes about 2 hours. It covers 11 progressive steps: consumer/provider setup, contract generation and verification (steps 1-5), missing-product and state-management scenarios (steps 6-7), authorization and request filtering (steps 8-10), and Pact Broker integration for cross-team publishing (step 11), built around a realistic e-commerce product-catalog scenario. Useful as the Java-ecosystem counterpart to the JS workshop already listed, for readers working in that stack.

members.description: Write a concrete breakage that a consumer-driven contract test catches and an integration test misses, and one the reverse. Then name a class of failure neither catches. The third answer is the one that shows you understand what contract testing actually buys.

principle: The entire offset model follows from Kafka keeping the broker stateless and pushing all consumption bookkeeping onto the client
because: The original design pushed all per-consumer state off the broker and onto the client, which is what let Kafka collapse a consumer's progress into one integer; that same collapse is what forces the API to distinguish the read position from the committed position and to insist you commit the next offset rather than the last one, since a single number can't represent 'processed' and 'safe to resume from' separately unless the convention pins down exactly which one it means.

members.subject: Partition-to-consumer exclusivity
members.description: The javadoc states the assignment invariant directly: 'if there is a topic with four partitions, and a consumer group with two processes, each process would consume from two partitions.' This exclusivity is what gives Kafka in-order, non-duplicated delivery per partition within a group -- two members of the same group never read the same partition concurrently. It also caps useful parallelism: a group cannot usefully have more active consumers than the topic has partitions, because the excess consumers will be assigned zero partitions.

members.subject: session.timeout.ms / heartbeat.interval.ms is a failure-detection-speed vs false-eviction tradeoff
members.description: session.timeout.ms (broker-side default 45s at the time reviewed) is how long the group coordinator waits without a heartbeat before declaring a member dead and triggering a rebalance; heartbeat.interval.ms (default 3s) is how often the client sends heartbeats, and is recommended at no more than 1/3 of session.timeout.ms so a few missed heartbeats don't immediately trip eviction. This is a judgment call, not a fixed-answer setting: a shorter session.timeout.ms detects genuinely crashed consumers faster (less downstream lag before another member takes over their partitions), but it also raises false-positive evictions during normal but momentarily slow behavior -- a GC pause, a slow disk flush, a brief CPU spike -- which then trigger a full rebalance for a consumer that was never actually dead. A related documented failure mode is a rebalance that never stabilizes: Kafka bug KAFKA-2985 records a consumer group that, after a load-test-induced session-timeout wave, kept re-forming with a new generation number over and over (generations 16 through 24+) rather than settling, with members hitting UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID and being unable to commit -- the ticket was closed as 'Not A Problem,' i.e. treated as expected behavior of the protocol under sustained heartbeat loss rather than a bug to fix, which is itself the trap: practitioners expect a rebalance storm to self-heal quickly and it is not guaranteed to. members.subject: Consumer group membership
members.description: All KafkaConsumer instances that share the same group.id belong to one consumer group. Kafka's broker-side group coordination automatically balances the partitions of subscribed topics among the live members of the group, so a group functions as a single logical subscriber even though it is made of many processes. This is the mechanism that lets consumption scale horizontally: adding more consumer processes to the same group.id increases parallelism without any application-level coordination code.

principle: A Terraform plan is a captured, time-bound authorization, not a preview
because: Applying a saved plan file happens without prompting because passing the file is itself the approval — this is what turns the four-step init/plan/review/apply pipeline into a real control rather than a formality, and why reviewers must see plan output itself rather than an HCL diff. Manual review is where destructive changes get a human gate; the saved artifact carrying that approval is itself sensitive; and a reviewed plan going stale, together with the GitLab incident where 617 resources were destroyed by applying a plan approved three weeks earlier, shows what happens when the authorization is exercised after the world it was captured against has already changed.

members.subject: Standard CI/CD pipeline: init, plan, human review, apply
members.description: HashiCorp's automation guidance defines the core Terraform pipeline as four ordered steps: initialize the working directory, produce a plan, have a human operator review that plan for acceptability, and only then apply the changes described by the plan.

members.subject: Reviewing plan output, not just HCL diffs, before merge
members.description: For a team, the value of terraform plan is as a review artifact, not just a preview: pairing plan output with the pull request lets reviewers see exactly what will change, ask questions, and catch mistakes that reading the HCL diff alone would miss, since HCL changes and their real infrastructure effects aren't always obvious from the code.

members.subject: Manual plan review is recommended whenever changes could be destructive
members.description: HashiCorp's own automation guidance states that manual review of a plan is always recommended when Terraform could make destructive changes to infrastructure, unless the team can tolerate downtime from an unintended change — auto-approval is not the default recommendation for anything where damage is possible.

members.subject: Applying a saved plan file is unprompted; passing the file is the approval
members.description: The pipeline shape in T3-020 (init, plan, human review, apply) is only sound if apply consumes the reviewed artifact rather than recomputing one. Terraform supports this by writing a plan to a file with plan -out=FILE and applying that file directly, and when a saved plan file is passed to terraform apply, Terraform performs the operations in that saved plan without prompting for confirmation -- the docs state that passing the plan file is itself interpreted as the approval. This is the operational rule that makes plan/apply review discipline mean anything, and it is also why a stale saved plan executes with no second gate in front of it (see T3-023 and the GitLab incident in T3-037): the approval was captured weeks earlier, at plan time.

members.subject: Saved plan files store sensitive data in cleartext
members.description: A saved Terraform plan file contains the full configuration, all planned values, and all plan options including input variables. If any of that data is sensitive — even if Terraform obscures it in terminal output — it is written to the plan file in cleartext, so saved plan files must be handled as sensitive artifacts (e.g., in CI/CD storage or artifact caches). [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment: what a reader loses without this row is the knowledge that CI artifact retention is an access-control decision -- a choice made once whose failure is invisible at the moment it's made and surfaces only when the artifact store is later read by someone who shouldn't have access. That is judgment's late-surfacing signature, not operation's immediate one. Applied for consistency with T3-003, which Stage 2 already moved to judgment on the identical reasoning (Terraform writes secrets in cleartext, so control access to it).]

members.subject: A reviewed plan can go stale before apply runs
members.description: HashiCorp's docs warn that other changes to the target system made in the time between generating a speculative plan and actually applying it can cause the real effect of an apply to differ from what the earlier plan indicated — a direct risk for review workflows where plan and apply are separated in time.

members.subject: An out-of-sync plan applied late causes mass unintended deletion

members.subject: HashiCorp tutorial: Automate Terraform with GitHub Actions
members.description: Official hands-on tutorial building a two-workflow GitHub Actions pipeline against an HCP Terraform workspace: one workflow generates a speculative plan on every pull request for review, the other applies on merge to main, using HashiCorp's own tfc-workflows-github actions and a real HCP Terraform team token.

members.subject: Drill: build a plan-on-PR/apply-on-merge pipeline with OIDC auth and a mandatory human-review gate
members.description: Wire a CI pipeline (e.g. GitHub Actions) that runs `terraform plan` on every pull request and posts the plan output itself — not just the HCL diff — as a reviewable PR artifact (T3-042), gates `apply` behind required human approval whenever the plan shows a destructive change (T3-021), and authenticates to the cloud provider via short-lived OIDC-issued credentials rather than static keys (T3-024–T3-027). principle: Standing access versus run-scoped access, applied at every layer of CI/CD credentialing
because: T-019's seven-step OIDC exchange, T-041's case for preferring it over static keys, and T-050's drill converting a pipeline from one to the other are all instances of a single tradeoff that T-044's stored-token tutorial sits on the opposite side of and T-045's tutorial sits on the OIDC side of: whether the CI/CD pipeline holds a standing secret that exists independent of any run, or a credential scoped to and torn down with the run that requested it.

members.subject: OIDC token exchange mechanics for dynamic credentials
members.description: The dynamic credentials flow: (1) HCP Terraform generates an OIDC-compliant workload identity token containing info about the organization, workspace/Stack, and run stage; (2) the token is sent to the cloud platform with auth details; (3) the cloud platform verifies the token using HCP Terraform's public signing key; (4) on success, the platform returns fresh temporary credentials; (5) these are configured in the run environment; (6) the plan or apply executes; (7) the run environment is torn down and credentials discarded. Self-hosted agents require v1.7.0+ to support this.

members.subject: Choosing OIDC over static long-lived credentials for CI/CD
members.description: A walkthrough of wiring GitHub Actions to AWS for Terraform notes that with static AWS access keys stored as CI secrets, 'anyone with access to the CI/CD logs can easily use the echo command and retrieve them,' that such keys 'needed to be rotated frequently - ideally weekly or monthly - to limit the window of compromise,' and that even with rotation they 'remained active between deployments, increasing the risk of misuse.' OIDC instead issues temporary, scoped credentials that 'automatically expire once the workflow is complete' and are bound to the specific workflow run, removing the standing-access window static keys create.
