T-041's underlying claim (re-verified this turn) is correct; only this drill's demonstration step is broken.]

principle: CLI workspaces share one backend, so they cannot substitute for real environment isolation
because: That CLI workspaces multiplex several states under a single configuration is precisely the design fact that makes them unable to give different environments separate credentials or access controls, and HashiCorp's recommended fix — separate configurations per environment sharing logic through modules — only makes sense once the mechanism and its limitation are seen as cause and effect rather than two independent claims about workspaces.

members.subject: CLI workspaces hold multiple states per configuration
members.description: A Terraform backend starts with a single default workspace containing one state. Backends that support multiple named workspaces let more than one state be associated with the same configuration, which is the mechanism CLI workspaces use.

members.subject: Workspaces are unsuitable for environment/credential separation
members.description: HashiCorp explicitly states that CLI workspaces are not the right tool when you need to decompose systems or when different deployments require separate credentials and access controls — a common misuse at team scale is treating workspaces as environment isolation when they don't provide that isolation. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-040 ("Workspaces vs. separate directories for environment isolation"), which made the identical core claim — CLI workspaces share one backend and cannot isolate credentials/access across environments — citing an adjacent sentence from the CLI workspaces doc. See merge log.]

members.subject: Separate configurations are the documented alternative to workspaces
members.description: Rather than using CLI workspaces for distinct environments, HashiCorp's own CLI docs recommend building reusable modules for the shared logic and instantiating each environment as its own separate configuration pointed at a different backend — because workspaces within one working directory share a single backend and are therefore not an isolation mechanism for credentials.

members.subject: Drill: convert an environment-by-CLI-workspace setup into separate configurations per environment
members.description: Start with a single root module and use `terraform workspace new` to create dev/staging/prod workspaces against one shared backend and one set of provider credentials. Identify concretely what this setup cannot do — scope IAM permissions differently per environment, or isolate one environment's state operations from another's (T3-010) — then refactor into separate per-environment root configurations, each with its own backend key and credentials, sharing common logic through a reusable child module (T3-011), exactly as HashiCorp's own CLI docs recommend as the alternative to workspaces.

principle: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire, not by name, and that single fact generates its entire safety discipline
because: Numbers being the actual wire identity is why reuse silently corrupts data instead of erroring, why deletion requires reservation rather than plain removal, why the wire-safe/unsafe tiering exists as a lookup table keyed to that same wire behavior, and why marking a field required creates a one-way commitment no future version can retract; the compare-drill only resolves once a reader can state that Avro matches by name and Protobuf by number.

members.subject: Protobuf field numbers are permanent wire identifiers
members.description: This is the single most load-bearing operation-level rule in Protobuf schema evolution: field names can be freely changed (they don't appear on the wire at all, only in generated source), but field numbers are the actual identity of a field to any decoder, old or new. Violating it doesn't produce a compile error - it silently corrupts data at runtime, which is exactly the kind of immediate-but-easy-to-miss failure that defines the operation tier.

members.subject: Protobuf field number reuse
members.description: Protobuf's own best-practices documentation states this without qualification: 'Never re-use a tag number. It messes up deserialization... Even if you think no one is using the field, don't re-use a tag number.' The mechanism: protobuf's wire format encodes only the field number and wire type, not the field name, so a message encoded under one schema and decoded under another that reassigned that number will silently misinterpret the bytes rather than erroring. The corrective governance practice, confirmed both in protobuf.dev and in Buf's breaking-change tool documentation (opened directly), is to mark deleted field numbers as `reserved` so the compiler itself blocks accidental reuse. Buf's `FIELD_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NUMBER_RESERVED` rule mechanically enforces this at CI time rather than relying on developer memory.

members.subject: Protobuf reserved fields prevent number/name reuse after deletion
members.description: This directly operationalizes the field-number-permanence rule from the companion row: deleting a field without reserving its number leaves a trap for a future developer who might unknowingly reassign that number to an unrelated field, which would then be misinterpreted by any old client still emitting the deleted field's data under the old number. Reserving both the numeric tag and the textual name closes both halves of that gap.

members.subject: Protobuf's tiered classification of changes: wire-safe, wire-unsafe, and conditionally-safe
members.description: This three-way classification is itself a judgment tool: the middle band ('wire-compatible' but requiring careful rollout) is where teams get burned, because the change type-checks and appears safe in isolation, but produces different results depending on which side (producer or consumer) upgrades first - the cost of getting the rollout order wrong surfaces at scale, not in a single local test. Choosing to make one of these conditionally-safe changes without a deliberate rollout plan is exactly the kind of correct-syntax-wrong-decision failure that defines judgment-level knowledge. [AUDIT depth judgment->operation: Protobuf's wire-safe / wire-unsafe / conditionally-safe classification is the lookup table you need to make a schema change correctly in the normal case; without it the change breaks immediately and visibly at decode. Its siblings A-020, A-021 and A-026 are all operation. (Arguable: the conditionally-safe band carries rollout-ordering judgment; better to split that out than to tier the whole row up.)]

members.subject: Protobuf required fields
members.description: Protobuf's official best-practices guide advises: 'Never add a required field, instead add // required to document the API contract' (i.e., convey the requirement in a comment/convention, not the wire schema). The rationale given is about the direction time moves in schema evolution: a field that seems logically required today may need to become optional or removed years later, and once a field is wire-level required, no future version can safely drop that requirement without breaking every client still enforcing it — an intentionally stricter feature becomes a one-way door. Teams that reach for `required` because it look like better data-quality enforcement are trading a short-term validation win for a long-term evolution hazard.

members.subject: Run the same schema change through Avro and Protobuf
members.description: Add a field, remove a field, rename a field, and change a field's type. For each, decide safety under Avro's resolution rules and under Protobuf's wire rules. The differences are not arbitrary: Avro resolves by name against a reader schema, Protobuf resolves by field number on the wire. Being able to state that sentence is the exit condition.

principle: Every route around state locking reopens the exact hazard locking exists to prevent
because: Automatic locking on writes and the hard stop on failed acquisition define the intended safety model, but every deviation from it — an opt-in backend feature nobody configured, a lock cleared while genuinely held, the -lock=false flag, or even a backend locking reads it was never supposed to touch — reintroduces or misapplies the same concurrent-writer corruption risk, a pattern only visible once the deviations are read against each other rather than as isolated facts.

members.subject: State locking is automatic when supported
members.description: When the configured backend supports it, Terraform automatically locks state for any operation that could write to it, which prevents a second concurrent operation from acquiring the lock and corrupting state.

members.subject: Lock acquisition failure halts the run
members.description: If Terraform cannot acquire the state lock, it does not proceed with the operation at all — it stops rather than attempting to run unsafely against state someone else may be writing to.

members.subject: S3 backend native state-lockfile locking is opt-in, not automatic
members.description: State locking on the S3 backend is opt-in, not automatic, and as of current docs is implemented via a lockfile mechanism configured with the use_lockfile argument, distinct from the older DynamoDB-table-based approach. A team that copies a bare S3 backend block without adding either gets zero protection against concurrent writers and won't discover it until two applies collide. [Stage 2 depth correction: reclassified from mechanism to operation after merging a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-038, which cited the identical quote at depth operation. See merge log.]

members.subject: Read-only Terraform commands can still block on a held state lock
members.description: HashiCorp's documentation says Terraform locks state "for all operations that could write state," but the etcdv3 backend locked on pure read operations like terraform state list and terraform show too, contradicting that description and blocking teammates from even inspecting state while a lock was held elsewhere; HashiCorp closed the report as not planned rather than aligning the backend's behavior.

members.subject: force-unlock risk of multiple writers
members.description: Terraform provides a force-unlock command for clearing a stuck lock, but HashiCorp's own docs warn that unlocking state while someone else genuinely holds the lock can result in multiple concurrent writers corrupting state — this is a judgment call about whether a lock is actually stale versus actively held. [Stage 2: absorbed a true duplicate from Stage 1B, T3-035 ("force-unlock on someone else's active lock can corrupt state"), which cited the identical quote from the same source. See merge log.]

members.subject: -lock=false silently removes the concurrency safety net
members.description: Most Terraform commands accept -lock=false to skip acquiring the state lock; it's offered as an escape hatch for a stuck pipeline, but HashiCorp's own documentation explicitly recommends against it because it reopens the exact concurrent-write risk locking exists to prevent. [ABSENCE (3B) depth operation->judgment, for consistency: T3-006 (force-unlock on a held lock -> multiple writers) and this row (-lock=false -> the same multiple-writer hazard) cite the same doc page about the same hazard and had landed at different levels. -lock=false runs successfully; the concurrent-write damage surfaces later, which is judgment. T3-006 was the correctly-assigned one.]

members.subject: Drill: reproduce and recover from a state lock collision
members.description: Stand up a local backend or a scratch S3 bucket without locking enabled and run two overlapping `terraform apply` processes against the same state to observe a corrupted or conflicting write. Reconfigure the backend with locking on (e.g. S3's use_lockfile) and repeat, observing the second run correctly blocked with a lock-acquisition error instead. Finally, kill the first process mid-run to leave a stale lock, and practice diagnosing from the lock info (who holds it, since when) whether it is actually safe to force-unlock before running that command — the judgment call the cluster's sources (T3-006, T3-035) warn is easy to get wrong under pressure.

principle: The dependency graph, not the order resources are written in HCL, is what Terraform actually walks
because: Meta-nodes existing only to represent count-expanded instances, and up to ten graph nodes executing concurrently rather than in file order, both point to the same underlying fact — the graph, addressed by node identity, is the real unit of execution — which is also why changing a resource's identity scheme from a numeric count index to a string for_each key looks like a cosmetic meta-argument edit but is actually a change the graph must resolve as two different objects, forcing destroy-and-recreate absent an explicit moved block.

members.subject: Dependency graph: resource meta-nodes represent count expansion
members.description: In Terraform's internal dependency graph, a resource meta-node does not represent an action on its own — it exists only to represent a group of resources, and only appears when a resource block has a count parameter greater than one, standing in for the set of expanded instances. [ABSENCE (3B) note, no grade change: dependency-graph count-expansion meta-nodes are not clearly inside the declared boundary (remote state, module design, multi-env CI/CD, workspaces, OIDC, drift, plan/apply review) -- flagged as a scope-drift observation, not a defect. Also cites developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/graph, which may describe a pre-current graph model; not independently re-verified this run.]

members.subject: Graph execution runs concurrently, not strictly sequentially
members.description: Terraform does not walk its dependency graph one node at a time by default — up to 10 nodes are processed concurrently as their dependencies are satisfied, and this concurrency limit is configurable via the -parallelism flag, which explains why plan/apply operations on independent resources can interleave.

members.subject: Switching a resource from count to for_each rebuilds it
members.description: Changing a resource or module call's meta-argument from count to for_each changes its state address from a numeric index (e.g. [1]) to a string key (e.g. ["1"]); Terraform treats these as different objects, so the plan shows the old instance destroyed and a new one created rather than an in-place rename, unless a moved block tells Terraform they're the same object. [VERIFY gap, caught by 3B in passing / missed by 3A: the stored quote is a GitHub issue TITLE phrased as a question ("When I change count to for_each, the resource will rebuild ?"), not an assertive statement -- it does not itself support the row's factual claims about state addressing and destroy/recreate behavior. The underlying claim is very likely true (it matches Terraform's documented addressing model) but the quote as stored fails the v0.3 contract: a quote that cannot support its claim signals the claim needs a better source or authored-with-inference labeling, per the Stage 1B brief. 3A's mechanical quote-check should have caught this and did not -- recorded as a real gap in the Haiku verify pass, not a false alarm.]

principle: Terraform only sees drift the instant something asks it to look
because: Health assessments scheduling periodic refresh-only plans, the configuration-drift-versus-state-drift distinction, the operational gap of having no automatic detection, and the refresh-only-plus-import reconciliation tutorial all trace back to the same architectural fact: Terraform is a pull-based, run-triggered tool with no standing watch on real infrastructure, so every practice here exists solely to manufacture the moment of looking that Terraform will never generate on its own.

members.subject: Health assessments / automated drift detection mechanics
members.description: HCP Terraform health assessments run periodic, non-actionable refresh-only Terraform plans in configured workspaces to compare real infrastructure against the state file. A health assessment never interrupts or interferes with runs - if a new run starts during an assessment, the assessment cancels and reschedules. Requirements: Terraform 0.15.4+ for drift detection alone (1.3.0+ for drift plus continuous validation), remote or agent execution mode, and the workspace's latest run must have been successful. Available only in Standard and Premium HCP Terraform editions.

members.subject: Configuration drift vs. state drift distinction
members.description: HCP Terraform's docs draw an explicit distinction: 'Configuration drift differs from state drift. Drift detection does not detect state drift.' Configuration drift is a mismatch between real infrastructure and the Terraform configuration; state drift involves external changes that don't necessarily invalidate configuration. When configuration drift is found, HCP Terraform proposes the changes needed to bring infrastructure back in sync with configuration.

members.subject: Assuming Terraform detects drift automatically
members.description: A long-time Terraform user's GitHub issue lists 'no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation' as a core operational gap: detecting drift requires manually running terraform plan (or -refresh-only), and 'automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable' when configuration is complex. Terraform does not watch infrastructure and flag changes on its own - someone or something has to run a plan for drift to surface at all. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the second quoted phrase is not a quotation. The row presents "automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable" in quotation marks as source text; the GitHub issue (hashicorp/terraform#31736) instead says 'You cannot reliably implement a cron job, because a lot of times an automatic Terraform apply can fail.' A paraphrase presented as a quotation, with a substituted rationale ('when configuration is complex' vs. the source's 'an automatic Terraform apply can fail'). The first quoted phrase ('no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation') is verbatim-correct and the headline claim stands.]

members.subject: Detecting and reconciling drift with -refresh-only and import
members.description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Manage resource drift.' Provisions an EC2 instance, key pair, and security group with Terraform, then intentionally introduces drift by modifying the security group via the AWS CLI outside Terraform. Detects the change with terraform plan -refresh-only, applies the refresh to sync state without touching infrastructure, imports a manually-created security group into management, then runs terraform apply to reconcile configuration and infrastructure, verifying with SSH/HTTP checks.

members.subject: Drill: drift detection and configuration-drift-vs-state-drift classification
members.description: Provision a small resource set with Terraform (e.g. a security group and an EC2 instance). Outside Terraform, make two separate changes: (1) modify a resource attribute directly via the cloud CLI (configuration drift - the live resource no longer matches your .tf files), and (2) construct a scenario where the state file alone diverges from configuration without any live change (state drift, per T-025's distinction). Run `terraform plan -refresh-only` to detect and apply the refresh for case (1), then explain in one sentence why the same command would not have caught case (2) - grounding your answer in T-025's stated distinction that 'drift detection does not detect state drift.' [AUDIT viable->wounded: case (2) teaches a definition its own cited row contradicts. The drill asks the reader to 'construct a scenario where the state file alone diverges from configuration without any live change (state drift, per T-025's distinction)' -- but T-025 and its source (HCP health-assessments docs) define state drift as external changes to real infrastructure that do not invalidate configuration, i.e. still a live change. A state file diverging from configuration with no live change is just an ordinary pending change any 'terraform plan' reports, not state drift, and is not constructible as described. Case (1) (configuration drift via cloud CLI, detected with -refresh-only) is sound and stands on its own.]

principle: Terraform infers resource identity from address or index, never from intent
because: T-037's count-based collections track resources by list position, so removing one element shifts every later index and makes Terraform touch resources nobody changed; T-038's address-based tracking treats a rename as delete-and-recreate unless a moved block says otherwise - different mechanisms, but the same underlying fact: Terraform never infers 'this is still the same resource' from context, only from an explicit key, and both traps are what happens when a team assumes it does.

members.subject: count versus for_each for resource collections
members.description: When resources are created from a list using the count meta-argument, removing an element from the middle of that list shifts the index of every subsequent element. Because count tracks resources in state by index number, this causes Terraform to plan changes to (and can destroy/recreate) resources that were never actually modified. for_each avoids this because it tracks resources by a consistent key rather than position, so removing one element only affects that element's resource. HashiCorp's own help-center article demonstrates this with a plan comparison: for_each destroys only the removed item, count modifies several and destroys one.

members.subject: Refactoring resource/module addresses without a moved block
members.description: By default, Terraform interprets a changed resource or module address (e.g. from a rename) as an instruction to destroy the existing object and create a new one at the new address, per HashiCorp's own docs. A moved block tells Terraform the existing state should follow the address change instead, avoiding the destroy/recreate. The docs also warn that removing a previously-added moved block later is itself a breaking change, since any config still pointing at the old address will then plan to delete rather than move: HashiCorp recommends retaining historical moved blocks to preserve the upgrade path for module users.

principle: A module's boundary is set by the abstraction it introduces, not by the resources it happens to wrap
because: The guidance to keep modules opinionated and single-purpose, the composition pattern where dependencies are received rather than created, the warning against thin wrappers that add no real concept, and the exam-prep and refactoring drills that rehearse this boundary-drawing skill are the same design discipline applied at different stages: a module earns its existence only when it names a concept the underlying provider resources do not already name on their own.

members.subject: Modules should be opinionated and single-purpose
members.description: HashiCorp's module-creation pattern guidance says a good module does one thing well and is deliberately opinionated; if you struggle to explain what a module's purpose is, that itself signals the module has taken on too much complexity to be reusable.

members.subject: Composition: modules receive dependencies rather than embedding them
members.description: In the composition pattern, a module does not create and manage its own private copy of a dependency; instead it receives that dependency as an input from the root module. This is what lets the same root module wire the same child modules together differently to produce different systems.

members.subject: Avoid thin-wrapper modules; raise the abstraction level
members.description: A well-designed module should introduce a new concept in your architecture built out of underlying provider resource types, rather than being a thin wrapper around a single resource type that adds no real abstraction.

members.subject: Terraform Associate practice exercises (state, modules, meta-arguments)
members.description: A third-party GitHub Pages set of six hands-on exercises for Terraform Associate prep covering AWS/GCP: first configuration, variables/outputs, resource dependencies, working with state (remote state and state locking), modules (creation/versioning/registry), and meta-arguments (count, for_each, lifecycle, dynamic blocks). Each exercise directory includes a README and a working solution.

members.subject: Drill: refactor a mega-module into scoped, composed modules
members.description: Take a single flat root configuration that manages several unrelated pieces of infrastructure as one module (e.g. a VPC, a compute service, and a database). Split it into separate modules scoped by HashiCorp's own encapsulation, privilege, and volatility criteria (T3-013); wire them together via composition, with the root module passing outputs as inputs rather than any module embedding its own provider or a dependency it doesn't own (T3-016); keep nesting to no more than two levels (T3-014); and audit the result for thin-wrapper modules — any module that is just one resource with no real abstraction — eliminating or merging them (T3-017).

principle: Parallel execution is safe only because graph construction already resolved dependencies and cycles first
because: The 9-phase construction in T-027 adds nodes, wires depends_on and interpolation edges, and validates a single acyclic root before any walk begins; T-028's depth-first-with-parallelism traversal and its default concurrency of 10 are only correct because that validation already happened - the concurrency knob is safe to turn precisely because it operates on a graph whose ordering constraints were proven, not assumed.

members.subject: Dependency graph: node types and 9-phase construction
members.description: Terraform builds a dependency graph and uses it to perform operations like generating plans and refreshing state. The graph contains resource nodes (one per instance when count is used), provider configuration nodes, and resource meta-nodes (convenience groupings for count>1 that don't represent actions). Construction proceeds through 9 phases: add resource nodes with diff/state metadata; link resources to provisioners; add explicit depends_on edges; incorporate orphaned resources present in state but not configuration; connect resources to provider config nodes; parse interpolations for implicit dependencies from resource-attribute references; add a root node pointing to all resources; split destroy/create nodes when diffs exist (since destroy order often differs from create order); and validate no cycles exist and there is a single root.

members.subject: Dependency graph: depth-first parallel execution, default concurrency 10
members.description: Terraform walks the dependency graph via a standard depth-first traversal, but with parallelism: 'a node is walked as soon as all of its dependencies are walked,' enabling concurrent operations while respecting dependency constraints. The default concurrency limit is 10 simultaneous nodes, adjustable via the -parallelism flag on plan, apply, and destroy. The docs describe changing it as 'an advanced operation' that 'should not be necessary for normal usage.'

principle: Avro resolves schemas by matching field names, and every Avro capability or failure here is a direct consequence of that one choice
because: Aliases exist because name-matching alone cannot distinguish a rename from a delete-plus-add; defaults exist to fill the gap name-matching leaves when a field is genuinely missing; the enum default symbol solves the identical gap for enum values instead of fields; and the trap's asymmetric error behavior (writer-only fields are silently ignored, reader-only fields without defaults error) falls directly out of resolving by name rather than position or number.

members.subject: Avro schema resolution: structural matching and type promotion
members.description: This is the mechanical rulebook a reader must follow to deserialize Avro data correctly whenever writer and reader schemas differ, which is the normal case in any evolving system - so it is operation-level, not orientation, because getting it wrong produces an immediate, visible deserialization failure or misread value. The specification is explicit that 'a reader must use the schema used by the writer' as an input to resolution, i.e. Avro readers need both schemas, unlike self-describing formats.

members.subject: Avro aliases allow renaming fields without breaking readers
members.description: Without aliases, renaming a field would be indistinguishable to the resolution algorithm from removing one field and adding an unrelated one (since matching is by name) - which would silently lose data rather than fail loudly. Aliases are the specific mechanism that makes renaming a compatible, correctly-round-tripping change instead of a data-loss trap.

members.subject: Avro field defaults enable safe field addition and removal
members.description: This is the concrete mechanism behind 'you can add or remove Avro fields compatibly': addition is safe if the new field carries a default (so old data missing it resolves to the default), and removal is safe because the reader ignoring an unknown writer field never fails. Field order in the schema does not matter for resolution - the spec explicitly notes fields are matched by name, so reordering a schema's field list is itself a non-breaking, cosmetic change.

members.subject: Avro enum default symbol enables forward-evolution of enums
members.description: This behavior is mechanism-level: it doesn't affect the normal case where every consumer already knows every enum value, so nobody encounters it operationally under everyday conditions. It only manifests in the novel situation of a producer emitting a newly-added symbol that a not-yet-upgraded consumer has never seen - exactly the scenario where a reader who only knows 'add fields with defaults' would incorrectly assume enums evolve the same way, or would be surprised the read doesn't simply throw. [AUDIT depth mechanism->operation: The Avro enum 'default' symbol is a concrete schema feature a reader applies, in the same class as A-007 (aliases) and A-008 (field defaults), both correctly at operation. Failure signature is 'you add an enum value and consumers break immediately and visibly', which is operation, not 'you cannot predict behavior you have not already seen'. Reads as assigned by how advanced 'schema resolution' sounds rather than against the failure-signature table.]

members.subject: Avro fields without default values
members.description: The Avro specification (opened directly) defines schema resolution precisely: if the reader's schema has a field with no matching field in the writer's schema and that reader field has no default value, 'an error is signalled' — not a null, not a skip. Default values are what let a reader schema fill in a value for a field the writer's schema didn't have. A second, less obvious point from the same spec: 'the presence of a default value does not make the field optional at encoding time. Avro encodes a field even if its value is equal to its default' — so a default solves the reader-compatibility problem but does not make the field optional for writers. The common mistake is adding a field to an Avro schema and assuming it's safe because Avro schemas 'support evolution' generically, without checking that the new field carries an explicit default. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Trap summary is symmetric: 'Adding OR REMOVING an Avro field without a default value breaks schema evolution outright.' The Avro specification says a writer field absent from the reader schema 'is ignored' -- removal never signals an error. Only the reader-has-a-field-with-no-default-that-the-writer-lacks direction gives 'an error is signalled.' A trap row that states its own rule imprecisely is worse than no trap; make the claim directional.]

members.subject: Confluent Schema Registry 101 — Evolve Existing Schemas hands-on
members.description: Confirmed by opening the page directly. Learner does two parallel tracks. Protobuf (UI): open the proto-purchase schema in Confluent Cloud Console, click 'Evolve Schema', add a new field (`string employee_id = 4;`), click 'Validate' to run the live compatibility check, save, and confirm the version incremented. Avro (local/CLI): edit purchase.avsc to add a field, run `./gradlew testSchemasTask` — which fails without a default value — then add `"default": "unknown"` and rerun until it succeeds, then run `./gradlew registerSchemasTask` to actually register the change. This is a genuinely hands-on exercise that makes the reader hit the exact failure this run's trap rows describe (Avro field with no default fails validation) and then fix it, rather than just reading about it. Part of the free Schema Registry 101 course on developer.confluent.io.

principle: Breaking-change classification is the single gate every downstream governance mechanism depends on
because: The Microsoft guidelines' definition of what counts as breaking, Buf's FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE/WIRE_JSON strictness ladder, Azure's review-board approval gate, and the Avro-versus-Protobuf field-resolution exercise are all downstream of one prior act: classifying a proposed change as breaking or safe. No tooling, human sign-off, or schema-evolution rule in the chain can run before that classification is made, which is why every mechanism here exists to enforce or automate it.

members.subject: Definition of a breaking change (Microsoft REST API Guidelines)
members.description: This is orientation-level: without this definition a reader cannot correctly classify any specific change as breaking or safe, which blocks everything downstream (versioning, deprecation, governance). Concrete examples the guidelines list as breaking: removing or renaming APIs or parameters, behavioral changes to existing APIs, changes to error codes and fault contracts, and anything that violates the 'principle of least astonishment.' The guidelines flag that even additive changes like new JSON response fields can break naive clients that do strict schema validation, which is why they insist each service publish its own explicit definition rather than relying on a universal one.

members.subject: Buf breaking change detection quickstart
members.description: Confirmed by opening the page directly. Three progressive, concrete exercises against a real example repo (buf.build/tutorials/breaking): (1) local git comparison — add a new enum value and run detection against uncommitted changes; (2) BSR module comparison — rename an enum value (`PET_TYPE_HAMSTER` to `PET_TYPE_RODENT`), which buf correctly flags as breaking with the exact message shown on the page; (3) remote git comparison — move an enum into a new file and discover this breaks under the default FILE ruleset but not under the looser PACKAGE ruleset, directly demonstrating the strictness-ladder concept (FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE_JSON/WIRE) rather than just asserting it. Squarely in scope for schema-evolution/breaking-change governance practice.

members.subject: Azure Breaking Change Review Board approval gate
members.description: This documents breaking-change governance as an organizational process, not just a technical rule: a human review board sits in the approval path specifically because the cost of an unreviewed breaking change surfaces late, at the customer's next deployment, not at merge time. Azure additionally requires an azure-deprecating response header communicating what is retiring, the retirement date, and a documentation URL - the same header-plus-link pattern as RFC 9745/8594, applied as a mandatory internal policy rather than an optional client courtesy. [AUDIT viable->wounded: 'pull requests failing the policy check cannot merge without that approval' is not in the cited Azure Guidelines.md -- the document contains no pull-request or merge-gating text. The review-board rule itself is quoted correctly ('DO NOT introduce any breaking changes into the service'; breaking changes 'allowable... if approved by the Azure Breaking Change Reviewers but only following ample communication to customers and a lengthy deprecation period'). Drop the unsupported merge-gate clause.]

members.subject: Buf's four breaking-change strictness categories: FILE, PACKAGE, WIRE, WIRE_JSON
members.description: Which category an organization enforces is a governance decision with different blast radii: FILE catches source-level breakage that would fail a compile in strict languages like C++ or Python, while WIRE only cares whether bytes on the wire still decode correctly, tolerating renames and file moves that would break generated code. Choosing a looser category than your actual consumers need is a decision whose cost surfaces later, when a change Buf approved as 'non-breaking' still breaks a consumer that depended on generated-code stability Buf wasn't checking for.

members.subject: Run the same schema change through Avro and Protobuf
members.description: Add a field, remove a field, rename a field, and change a field's type. For each, decide safety under Avro's resolution rules and under Protobuf's wire rules. The differences are not arbitrary: Avro resolves by name against a reader schema, Protobuf resolves by field number on the wire. Being able to state that sentence is the exit condition.

principle: Drift is invisible until something runs a plan, automated or not
because: T-039 establishes there is no ambient detection loop - Terraform only sees drift the moment something runs a plan; T-024's HCP health assessments are that same manual mechanism (refresh-only plans) running on a schedule rather than continuously, which is exactly why T-025's distinction holds: they catch configuration drift but not state drift, because both are still just a plan being run against real infrastructure; T-043 and T-052 are the same -refresh-only-and-import sequence demonstrated by hand, whether or not HCP is doing the scheduling.

members.subject: Health assessments / automated drift detection mechanics
members.description: HCP Terraform health assessments run periodic, non-actionable refresh-only Terraform plans in configured workspaces to compare real infrastructure against the state file. A health assessment never interrupts or interferes with runs - if a new run starts during an assessment, the assessment cancels and reschedules. Requirements: Terraform 0.15.4+ for drift detection alone (1.3.0+ for drift plus continuous validation), remote or agent execution mode, and the workspace's latest run must have been successful. Available only in Standard and Premium HCP Terraform editions.

members.subject: Configuration drift vs. state drift distinction
members.description: HCP Terraform's docs draw an explicit distinction: 'Configuration drift differs from state drift. Drift detection does not detect state drift.' Configuration drift is a mismatch between real infrastructure and the Terraform configuration; state drift involves external changes that don't necessarily invalidate configuration. When configuration drift is found, HCP Terraform proposes the changes needed to bring infrastructure back in sync with configuration.

members.subject: Assuming Terraform detects drift automatically
members.description: A long-time Terraform user's GitHub issue lists 'no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation' as a core operational gap: detecting drift requires manually running terraform plan (or -refresh-only), and 'automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable' when configuration is complex. Terraform does not watch infrastructure and flag changes on its own - someone or something has to run a plan for drift to surface at all. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the second quoted phrase is not a quotation. The row presents "automated reconciliation via cron jobs is unreliable" in quotation marks as source text; the GitHub issue (hashicorp/terraform#31736) instead says 'You cannot reliably implement a cron job, because a lot of times an automatic Terraform apply can fail.' A paraphrase presented as a quotation, with a substituted rationale ('when configuration is complex' vs. the source's 'an automatic Terraform apply can fail'). The first quoted phrase ('no in-built, pull-based, GitOps friendly, automatic drift detection and synchronisation') is verbatim-correct and the headline claim stands.]

members.subject: Detecting and reconciling drift with -refresh-only and import
members.description: Official HashiCorp tutorial: 'Manage resource drift.' Provisions an EC2 instance, key pair, and security group with Terraform, then intentionally introduces drift by modifying the security group via the AWS CLI outside Terraform. Detects the change with terraform plan -refresh-only, applies the refresh to sync state without touching infrastructure, imports a manually-created security group into management, then runs terraform apply to reconcile configuration and infrastructure, verifying with SSH/HTTP checks.

members.subject: Drill: drift detection and configuration-drift-vs-state-drift classification
members.description: Provision a small resource set with Terraform (e.g. a security group and an EC2 instance). Outside Terraform, make two separate changes: (1) modify a resource attribute directly via the cloud CLI (configuration drift - the live resource no longer matches your .tf files), and (2) construct a scenario where the state file alone diverges from configuration without any live change (state drift, per T-025's distinction). Run `terraform plan -refresh-only` to detect and apply the refresh for case (1), then explain in one sentence why the same command would not have caught case (2) - grounding your answer in T-025's stated distinction that 'drift detection does not detect state drift.' [AUDIT viable->wounded: case (2) teaches a definition its own cited row contradicts. The drill asks the reader to 'construct a scenario where the state file alone diverges from configuration without any live change (state drift, per T-025's distinction)' -- but T-025 and its source (HCP health-assessments docs) define state drift as external changes to real infrastructure that do not invalidate configuration, i.e. still a live change. A state file diverging from configuration with no live change is just an ordinary pending change any 'terraform plan' reports, not state drift, and is not constructible as described. Case (1) (configuration drift via cloud CLI, detected with -refresh-only) is sound and stands on its own.]

principle: Scoping state to limit blast radius creates a new seam, and crossing that seam leaks the whole snapshot
because: Keeping each workspace's state small and scoped is a risk-containment decision that immediately creates a new problem — separated configurations still need each other's outputs — and terraform_remote_state is the documented way to get them; but because a state snapshot is one object in the backend rather than a narrow API, any principal who can read those outputs can also read the entire snapshot directly, secrets included, so the blast-radius fix and its cross-reference mechanism form a closed loop with a security hole at the join.

members.subject: Scoping state/workspace boundaries to limit blast radius
members.description: Because any write operation against a state file can affect every resource tracked in it, HCP Terraform's own guidance is to keep each workspace's state small and scoped to logically related resources rather than grouping unrelated infrastructure (e.g. compute and database) into one state file - the state boundary is a risk-containment decision, not just an organizational convenience.

members.subject: Reading another configuration's state with terraform_remote_state
members.description: The terraform_remote_state data source reads the latest state snapshot from another configuration's backend and exposes that configuration's root module output values to the caller. This is the mechanism that makes state decomposition workable: once a team follows the harvest's own advice to split state for blast-radius containment (T3-043) and to give each environment its own configuration and backend (T3-011), the separated configurations still need to reference each other's outputs, and this data source is the documented way to do it. The same page notes that only root-level output values are exposed -- resource data and nested-module outputs are not.

members.subject: Reading another team's outputs grants read access to their entire state snapshot
members.description: Granting a configuration access to another configuration's outputs via terraform_remote_state is not a narrow permission. The state snapshot is a single object in the backend, so any principal with enough access to read the root module output values can also read the full state snapshot by direct network requests. Combined with the fact that state stores secrets in plaintext (T3-031, T3-003), this means the decision to let team B consume team A's remote state is a decision to let team B read every secret in team A's infrastructure. HashiCorp's own docs recommend a separately published data store for cross-team values where that is not acceptable.

principle: The commit is Kafka's one true checkpoint, and every consumer guarantee falls out of when it fires
because: Auto-commit's silent data loss, the manual-commit duplicate window, the transaction coordinator's durable commit and abort markers, and the off-by-one hiding in committed-position semantics are not five separate issues. Each is the same atomic checkpoint mechanism observed at a different point in its lifecycle: Kafka defines exactly one instant at which 'done' becomes durable truth, and every delivery guarantee is simply a description of what can go wrong on either side of that instant.

members.subject: Auto-commit timing window
members.description: A widely repeated mistake is assuming auto-commit means 'Kafka safely tracks my progress for me.' In practice, the automatic commit fires on the next call to poll() and commits the offsets returned by the previous poll() -- it is decoupled from whether the consumer actually finished processing those records. If the consumer crashes after poll() returns a batch but before it finishes handling all records in that batch, the next commit (on the following poll or the commit interval, default 5s via auto.commit.interval.ms) may commit offsets past records that were never fully processed, silently dropping them from the at-least-once guarantee people assume auto-commit provides. A related, separately documented race: calling pause() during graceful shutdown while auto-commit is on can seek to stale cached offsets and overwrite correct committed offsets, causing already-processed messages to be reprocessed on restart. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Origin https://github.com/confluentinc/confluent-kafka-javascript/issues/404 is a client-library bug report: pause() seeks to a stale #lastConsumedOffsets entry and commits it immediately under enable.auto.commit=true. That is not the general 'auto-commit commits the offset from the last poll(), not the batch just processed' mechanism the row asserts. Related phenomenon, wrong mechanism. Repoint origin to the KafkaConsumer javadoc, which does support the claim.]

members.subject: At-least-once still requires an idempotent consumer, even with careful commit ordering
members.description: The standard at-least-once recipe is enable.auto.commit=false plus a manual commit issued only after the consumer has fully processed a batch's side effects. This closes the message-loss failure mode of auto-commit (never marking a message done before it's actually done) but does not and cannot close the duplicate-processing failure mode: if the process crashes or is rebalanced away after the side effect (e.g. a DB write or downstream publish) succeeds but before the offset commit is acknowledged, the next owner of that partition will start from the last committed offset and reprocess the already-applied message. This is why every at-least-once consumer that has externally visible side effects needs its own idempotency mechanism (dedup key, upsert semantics, idempotent API call) independent of anything Kafka's client does -- the guarantee Kafka gives is about redelivery, not about effects. [AUDIT viable->wounded: Origin https://tarkalabs.com/blogs/kafka-message-duplication/ describes duplicates arising from a poll-timeout eviction and rebalance ('Kafka will assume that the service is dead... the same message will then be assigned to, and processed by, another consumer in the group'), not from 'a crash between finishing processing and committing the offset' as the row asserts. The conclusion (at-least-once needs an idempotent consumer) is right and the article does present that solution; the stated mechanism is not the cited one.]

members.subject: Transaction coordinator, transaction log, and commit/abort markers
members.description: KIP-98 describes the three components that make multi-partition atomicity possible: applications need 'the ability to write to several TopicPartitions atomically... either all messages are committed, or none of them are.' Each transactional producer connects to a transaction coordinator, a broker role that assigns PIDs, tracks transaction state, and drives commit/abort. The transaction log is an internal Kafka topic that durably persists this metadata so in-flight transactions can be recovered after a coordinator failure. When the producer calls commitTransaction() or abortTransaction(), the coordinator writes a COMMIT or ABORT marker as a control message to every partition that participated in the transaction; consumers use these markers to decide whether to surface or discard the transactional messages that preceded them.

members.subject: Trace the loss and duplicate windows for each commit strategy
members.description: Write out a three-column table: auto-commit, sync-commit-after-process, sync-commit-before-process. For each, mark the instant a crash produces loss and the instant it produces a duplicate. The exercise is done when you can state which strategy gives at-most-once and which gives at-least-once without looking it up, and can point at the line of code where the window opens.

members.subject: Position vs committed position, and the n+1 commit rule
members.description: The KafkaConsumer javadoc is explicit that 'there are actually two notions of position relevant to the user of the consumer: The position of the consumer gives the offset of the next record that will be given out. It will be one larger than the highest offset the consumer has seen in that partition... The committed position is the last offset that has been stored securely. Should the process fail and restart, this is the offset that the consumer will recover to.' It then states the rule that manual-commit code gets wrong: 'Note: The committed offset should always be the offset of the next message that your application will read. Thus, when calling commitSync(offsets) you should use nextRecordToBeProcessed.offset() or if ConsumerRecords is exhausted already ConsumerRecords.nextOffsets() instead.' Committing record.offset() rather than record.offset()+1 does not fail loudly -- it silently reprocesses exactly one record per commit, forever, which is invisible in any test that tolerates at-least-once. The same section adds a second correction to the naive mental model: 'offsets are not guaranteed to be consecutive (such as compacted topic or when records have been produced using transactions)', so code that infers message loss from a gap in offsets is wrong. Added by audit: K-002 establishes that position is a single integer at orientation depth and K-006 covers commitSync vs commitAsync, but no row in the set states what value to commit.

principle: Everything that follows from state being a binding record, not a desired-state source of truth
because: T-002 establishes that state's only job is binding already-created objects to configuration and refreshing before any operation; T-006 shows plan literally performing that refresh-then-diff first; T-001 and T-008 only work because centralizing or read-only-sharing a binding record is safe in a way sharing a 'desired state' would not be; and T-035's incident is exactly what happens when a team assumes state itself is what apply converges toward instead of configuration.

members.subject: What a Terraform backend is
members.description: A backend defines where Terraform stores its state data files. The docs state: 'The backend defines where Terraform stores its state data files.' Backends allow state to be centrally stored so multiple team members can access and collaborate on the same infrastructure, rather than each person holding a local state file.

members.subject: Purpose of Terraform state
members.description: State's primary purpose is to store bindings between objects in a remote system and resource instances declared in configuration. Terraform uses state to determine what changes to make, and does a refresh prior to any operation to update state with real infrastructure. State also improves performance for large infrastructures by avoiding a full rescan on every operation. [AUDIT: source (developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state) supports the bindings claim and the refresh-before-operation claim verbatim, but does not state 'by avoiding a full rescan on every operation' as the performance mechanism -- that clause is an unsourced rationale (Prohibition 2).]

members.subject: terraform plan computation steps
members.description: terraform plan performs three sequential operations: it reads the current state of already-existing remote objects to make sure state is up to date, compares the current configuration to the prior state noting differences, then proposes a set of change actions that would make remote objects match configuration. Plan alone does not carry out the proposed changes - it is a preview for review before apply.

members.subject: Remote state sharing via terraform_remote_state
members.description: With remote state, Terraform writes state data to a remote data store shared between all team members, eliminating the need for each user to manually ensure they have the latest state and that nobody else is running Terraform simultaneously. The terraform_remote_state data source lets teams share output values read-only across configurations, allowing infrastructure to be decomposed into smaller, independently-managed components.

members.subject: Unmanaged out-of-band changes silently reverted by later applies
members.description: A support engineer manually upgraded a database SKU outside Terraform. Weeks later, an unrelated apply reverted the database back to the SKU still recorded in Terraform's state, affecting production - because Terraform's state, not the live resource, is its source of truth, and nothing had reconciled the two in between. [AUDIT viable->wounded: the row's causal mechanism is wrong and contradicts T-002/T-006 in the same file. The row claims the revert happened 'because Terraform's state, not the live resource, is its source of truth' -- but Terraform refreshes state from live infrastructure before planning (the source itself says 'Terraform saw the drift'). The revert happened because the CONFIGURATION still declared the old SKU, and apply converges toward configuration; state is the binding record, not the desired-state source of truth. As written the row teaches the reader the opposite of how plan/apply actually works. The incident itself (manual SKU change reverted by a later unrelated apply) is supported.]
